P2600.d: P2600 means the controller sees an open circuit on the line that drives electric coolant pump A, directly or through its relay. GM's 2023 ECM table tests the auxiliary coolant pump relay output while it is off: more than 200 kOhm for 5 of 6 seconds sets the code as Type B, so the MIL follows after two trips.
s: MIL or hybrid warning lamp on
Little or no cabin heat
Rising coolant temperature in hybrid or after-run operation
c: Internal open circuit in the electric pump or its electronics
Water or coolant ingress causing poor contact at the pump
Chafed or broken control wire, loose connector or failed relay
Coolant level too low (named by Hyundai as possible trigger)

P2601.d: P2601 is set when electric coolant pump A is commanded on, yet its feedback or its effect shows that it is not really working, while the wiring itself tests sound. GM's 2008 table for the 3.6 L LLT judges its auxiliary pump indirectly: after a shutdown with coolant above 110 °C the pump runs on, and if the coolant does not cool down as the ambient-dependent calibration expects within about 80 s, the code is logged.
s: MIL on
Weak cabin heating
Coolant temperature stays high after shutdown
c: Electric pump seized, worn or running too slowly
Control module software misjudging the pump (update available)
Air pocket or low coolant so the pump runs dry

P2602.d: P2602 reports that the control circuit of electric coolant pump A reads low - typically a ground short, or a matching fault report from the driver stage. Which pump is A varies: Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary defines it as the auxiliary pump of the high-temperature loop for cabin heating, checked continuously over 5 s above 11 V; GM's 2008 3.6 L LLT table uses an after-run pump (P2602 = circuit to ground, stor
s: Fault code stored; MIL depends on the maker (GM 2008 LLT table none, GM 2023 ECM table Type B)
Weak cabin heating
No after-run of the pump after a hot shutdown
c: Internal fault in the electric coolant pump or its electronics
Coolant or water ingress into the pump connector

P2603.d: P2603 means the drive line of electric coolant pump A reads high - usually a short to the supply side, or an overcurrent seen by the driver stage. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary assigns pump A to the auxiliary high-temperature loop for cabin heating and sets P2602/P2603 when the smart driver reports a fault within 5 s.
s: Fault code stored; MIL depends on the maker (GM 2008 LLT table none, GM 2023 ECM table Type B)
Weak cabin heating
Higher coolant temperature after hot shutdown
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Seized or sluggish pump drawing excessive current
Faulty driver stage in the ECM

P2604.d: P2604 is the functional check of intake air heater A - the grid heater in the intake that warms the charge air of a diesel engine for cold starts. The circuit responds, but current, voltage drop or heating effect do not match the command.
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
Check engine light
c: Worn or sticking intake air heater relay
Loose or burnt terminals on the heater supply cable
Degraded or partly open heater grid

P2605.d: P2605 points to an open circuit at intake air heater B, a second heating element in the intake of a diesel engine; the control unit finds no current path through the element, its relay or the cabling. Volvo's EMS code lists keep heaters A, B and C apart.
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke after a cold start
MIL on
c: Loose, corroded or burnt terminal at heater element or relay

P2606.d: P2606 means heater B in the intake does respond, but the current it draws or the voltage drop across its circuit lies outside the window the engine controller expects. Mack documents P2604-7F and P2606-7F for 2014-2017 trucks with MP7, MP8 and MP10 engines and puts them down to extra circuit resistance from corrosion inside the master disconnect switch, so inspecting those contacts comes first.
s: Sluggish cold starts
White smoke until the engine is warm
MIL on
c: Extra resistance from corroded contacts, e.g. in the master disconnect switch
Aged heater element with changed resistance
Outdated engine software (update published by the maker)

P2607.d: P2607 says the signal from the circuit of intake air heater B stays too low, which normally means a grounded control or feedback line, or a relay output pulled down. No manufacturer documents P2607 publicly.
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke after a cold start
MIL on
c: Control or feedback wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the preheat relay
Moisture or corrosion in a connector of the heater circuit

P2608.d: P2608 is logged when the circuit of intake air heater B reads too high, for instance a short to battery positive on the control line or a relay that stays energized when it should be off. Volvo is the one maker that names it in public bulletins: the August 2020 EMS change log for heavy-truck engines lists P2608-00 among the preheater codes reduced by a relay robustness update, and Volvo's 2022 instruction for the pre
s: MIL on
Batteries run down after short trips or standstill
Hard cold starts or white smoke
c: Preheat relay contacts welded or sticking closed
Control or feedback wire shorted to battery positive
Engine software needing the maker's update

P2609.d: P2609 judges the intake air heating as a whole rather than one circuit: the controller compares what the grid heater should achieve with what it measures, for example via the current drawn or the rise in intake air temperature during preheat. Ram has published two service documents for its 6.7 L Cummins pickups.
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke and rough idle after a cold start
MIL on
c: Worn heater grid or relay (replace as a set)
Overheated or loose supply cable between relay and grid
Engine software with an outdated diagnostic (reflash available)
Intake air temperature sensor reading implausibly

P260A.d: P260A reports an open circuit in the output a control module uses to engage the power take-off, typically the coil circuit of a PTO relay or engagement solenoid. GM's PTO module on 2008-2014 Silverado/Sierra 3500 HD chassis cabs, described in upfitter bulletin UI 80c, switches both the supply and the ground side of an upfitter-installed relay and refuses PTO operation unless both lines are connected; GM also notes th
s: PTO does not engage
PTO indicator flashes or stays off
c: Relay coil wiring missing, broken or only one side connected by the upfitter
Open coil in the PTO relay or engagement solenoid
Corroded or loose connector in the chassis wiring

P260B.d: P260B is stored when the PTO control output reads too low, the classic case being a grounded wire leading to the PTO relay coil. GM documents the code as P260B.00, a low voltage on the PTO relay control line, among the faults the PTO module can set on 2008-2014 Silverado and Sierra 3500 HD chassis cabs.
s: PTO cannot be engaged
Message or flashing PTO indicator
c: Relay control wire chafed against the frame or body
Shorted coil in the PTO relay or solenoid
Relay wired incorrectly during body installation

P260C.d: P260C signals that the PTO control output reads too high, usually because the relay control line touches a powered wire or the relay coil draws too much current. GM lists it as P260C.00, a high voltage on the PTO relay control line, in the diagnostic table of the PTO module that GM fitted to Silverado and Sierra 3500 HD chassis cab trucks from 2008 to 2014.
s: PTO will not engage or will not release
PTO indicator behaves abnormally
c: Relay control wire shorted to a powered circuit
Relay or solenoid coil with too low resistance
Faulty splice or add-on wiring from the body installation

P260D.d: P260D concerns the output that drives the lamp or LED telling the operator that the power take-off is engaged; the module has found a fault in that lamp circuit. For GM's heavy-duty pickup chassis cabs, upfitter bulletin UI 80c explains how such an indicator behaves: the LED in the PTO switch blinks quickly while the relay is energized, turns steady once load feedback confirms engagement or after 3 s without feedback
s: PTO indicator stays dark or lit regardless of PTO state
PTO itself works normally
c: Open or shorted wire to the indicator, often in add-on wiring
Fault in the PTO switch assembly with integrated LED

P260E.d: Diesel machines often have a separate dashboard lamp that tells the operator a particulate filter regeneration is needed or running. P260E covers the circuit that switches this lamp.
s: Regeneration lamp dark or permanently lit
Missed regeneration requests leading to high soot load
Later power reduction by the engine controller
c: Lamp wire shorted to ground or to supply
Lamp or bulb holder open, or lamp not fitted on this machine
Corroded connector at dashboard or engine controller

P260F.d: Some evaporative leak tests run long after the engine is switched off, so Ford gives them a small dedicated processor that works during the soak. P260F is set when that monitoring processor does not behave as intended.
s: MIL on
EVAP readiness not set, small leak test not completed
c: Internal fault in the EVAP monitoring processor or module
Supply, ground or CAN wiring fault at the monitoring module

P2610.d: Several emission monitors need to know how long the engine was off, for example to judge a cold start or an evaporative test after a soak. P2610 reports that the module's engine-off timer gives implausible values.
s: MIL on, usually without drivability change
Cold-start and EVAP monitors may not run
c: Engine module software prone to false timer faults (update available)
Battery disconnect, transport fuse removed or supply dropout during soak
Timer message from another module (e.g. cluster) missing on CAN
Internal timer fault in the control module

P2611.d: A refrigerant distribution valve is an electrically switched valve in the A/C circuit that opens or blocks the refrigerant path to one branch, for example a rear evaporator or a battery chiller. P2611 tells you the engine or powertrain module can no longer drive valve A because its control line or coil is open.
s: One A/C zone (e.g. rear) blows warm or cannot be shut off
Reduced battery cooling on hybrids or EVs, possibly limited charging power
Stored code, often without warning lamp
c: Valve solenoid coil burnt out or internally open
Corroded or loose connector at the valve, often near condensation
Broken control wire between module and valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P2612.d: P2612 is stored when the voltage on the drive line of refrigerant distribution valve A stays lower than the module expects, which normally points to a ground fault in the wire or inside the valve. Volkswagen is an unusual case: its engine control module reports P2612 as a ground short of the A/C compressor regulator valve N280, the electrically controlled valve of the variable-displacement compressor.
s: A/C does not cool or compressor does not engage (VW)
One cooling branch or zone remains inactive
Code stored, usually no other driveability symptom
c: Brittle or corroded connector at the valve (VW N280 plug near the starter)
Internal short in the valve coil

P2613.d: P2613 means the control circuit of refrigerant distribution valve A reads too high: the wire has a short to the supply side, or the driver stage senses excessive current when it switches the valve. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford lists only the open-circuit code P2611, and the VW use of P2612 refers to the compressor regulator valve.
s: An A/C branch keeps cooling although it should be off
Valve output switched off, so the branch does not work at all
Code stored without engine symptoms
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Valve coil with shorted windings drawing too much current
Defective driver in the controlling module

P2614.d: Some engine computers pass a copy of the camshaft position signal on to another module, for example an injector driver unit or a valve timing controller. P2614 means that this outgoing line for camshaft A on bank 1 is broken or its pulses never reach the receiver.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Long cranking or no-start
Engine stalls or misfires intermittently
c: Broken wire or loose terminal between sending module and receiving module
Camshaft sensor signal itself missing or out of sync with the crank signal
Receiving module (e.g. injector control module) not reading the signal
Defective output stage in the engine control module

P2615.d: P2615 points to a camshaft A (bank 1) position output line that the engine module finds pulled to ground. GM documents it for the Cadillac CT6 in its 2018 tables: with the driver switched off and the line commanded high, the ECM measures the voltage and flags a short at an impedance to ground of 0.5 ohm or less; at 200 kilohm or more it treats the circuit as open, and some controllers then log P2614 instead.
s: Stored code, often without warning lamp
Rough or delayed starting
Valve timing control in fallback mode
c: Output wire chafed through and touching ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the connector pins to ground
Internally shorted input in the receiving module
Faulty output driver in the engine control module

P2616.d: P2616 is the opposite fault to P2615: the outgoing camshaft A position line on bank 1 stays at supply potential although the module has switched its low-side driver on and wants the line low. In GM's 2018 CT6 tables the ECM declares a power short once the impedance toward the supply is 0.5 ohm or less, using the same window of 40 bad readings in 50 at 100 ms intervals, engine not cranking and at least 11 V; the code
s: Stored code without warning lamp
Hard starting or hesitation after start
Cam phasing faults logged by the receiving module
c: Output wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Low-side driver in the engine module no longer switching
Back-feed through a damaged or corroded connector

P2617.d: When an engine module relays the crankshaft position signal to another controller, P2617 says that this forwarded line is open or the pulses go missing at the receiver. Ford's 2003 6.0 L diesel summary describes the clearest case: the fuel injector control module counts a fault whenever the crank pulse it gets from the PCM is absent or does not line up with the camshaft signal, monitored continuously above 90 rpm, an
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine cranks but does not start
Sudden stalling while driving
c: Open wire or pushed-out pin on the crank output line
Crank sensor signal itself missing or out of sync with the cam signal
Receiving module (e.g. injector control module) faulty

P2618.d: P2618 reports a crankshaft position output line that is shorted to ground. GM uses it widely, from the 2011–2012 hybrid tables to the 2019 ECM summaries, wherever the engine module provides a crank position output.
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Related faults or substitute mode in the receiving module
Occasional hesitation or start problems
c: Harness pinched or chafed so the output touches ground
Water or corrosion in the output connector
Shorted input stage in the receiving module
Output driver failure in the engine control module

P2619.d: P2619 is set when the crankshaft position output line is held at supply voltage while the module's low-side driver is switched on and expects it to be pulled down. GM's 2014 hybrid ECM table treats an impedance of 0.5 ohm or less toward power as the fault and evaluates it like the low case: 40 failures in 50 samples every 100 ms, engine not cranking, relay voltage of 11 V or more, Type B with MIL after two trips.
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Receiving module reports implausible crank signal
Possible reduced power or start problems
c: Damaged insulation lets the output touch a positive feed
Low-side driver in the engine module failed open

P261A.d: P261A reports an open circuit in the drive of an auxiliary electric coolant pump labelled B. Ford's gasoline OBD summaries for 2020-2023 and 2024 define pump B as the high-temperature loop pump for component cooling and check it continuously over 5 s with at least 11 V on board.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only sporadically
No after-run circulation, heat soak after hot shutdown
Component temperatures (turbo, electronics) rise
c: Pump connector not fully seated or with spread terminals
Auxiliary pump with internal open (electronics or motor)
Broken supply or control wire, or failed relay where fitted

P261B.d: Unlike the wiring codes around it, P261B judges whether coolant pump B actually delivers when commanded. The verdict comes from pump feedback or from its effect on coolant temperatures, so the circuit can test fine while the pump does nothing.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine or turbo runs hotter after shutdown, possible boiling noises
Heater or component cooling weak in certain conditions
c: Auxiliary pump motor or electronics failing intermittently
Air pocket after coolant service, pump runs dry
Impeller blocked by debris or deposits

P261C.d: P261C points to a control line of coolant pump B pulled toward ground. VW's 2014 Touareg data book sets it when the signal voltage drops below 2.8-3.2 V.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Auxiliary pump does not run, no after-run cooling
Rising temperatures at turbo or electronics in heavy use
c: Chafed wire to ground near exhaust or engine parts
Internal short in the pump electronics, often after water ingress

P261D.d: With P261D the module finds the drive of coolant pump B too high, either a short to the supply side or a current above the permitted limit. VW's 2014 Touareg book uses a current test here, roughly 2.2 to 4 A as the threshold.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump switched off for protection or running permanently
Possible battery drain if the pump keeps running after shutdown
c: Stiff or partly seized pump drawing excess current
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Faulty driver stage in the engine module

P261E.d: P261E covers the case where coolant pump B keeps working although the module has commanded it off. That can be an output that stays energised, a relay with welded contacts, or, on switchable mechanical pumps, a shroud or valve that no longer closes, so coolant circulates during warm-up.
s: Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cool longer
Pump audible after the engine is switched off
Warning lamp and possibly a thermostat code
c: Pump relay with welded contacts or output stage stuck on
Switchable pump shroud or vacuum/solenoid valve not closing
Control line shorted to battery voltage

P261F.d: P261F means electric coolant pump A reports activity while the module has it switched off. GM's 2025 ECM table 25OBDG04B describes the test: with the pump commanded off or below 299 rpm for 2 s and more than 11 V on board, a feedback speed of 3,100 rpm or more for 8 of 10 seconds sets the code as Type B; the warning lamp follows on the second faulty trip.
s: Check engine lamp after two faulty trips
Usually no noticeable driveability change
Slower warm-up when the pump really keeps running
c: Impeller driven by main pump flow at high rpm, fixed by ECM software (GM)
Vacuum leak or contaminated switching valve of a switchable pump (Mercedes OM651)
Pump electronics reporting wrong speed or not switching off

P2620.d: P2620 concerns a line on which the engine module sends a throttle position value out to another unit, for instance a transmission or body controller, as an analogue or pulse-width signal. The code means the module detects that this output circuit is open, so the receiver gets nothing usable.
s: Stored code, warning lamp behaviour depends on the maker
Irregular shift points or idle control in the receiving module
c: Open wire or loose pin on the throttle position output line
Corroded connector at the sending or receiving module
Output stage in the engine control module defective

P2621.d: P2621 flags the throttle position output line as shorted to ground or reading below its permitted voltage band. A receiving module such as a transmission controller would then see a value that looks like a fully closed throttle all the time.
s: Stored code in the engine module
Receiver behaves as if the throttle were always closed (late or odd shifts)
c: Output wire chafed against body ground
Corrosion bridging the output pin to ground
Shorted input in the receiving module

P2622.d: P2622 means the throttle position output line sits too high, typically because it is shorted to a supply wire or the driver in the sending module cannot pull it down. The receiver would read a value resembling wide-open throttle even at idle, which can confuse shift scheduling or torque calculations.
s: Stored code in the engine module
Receiver acts as if at full throttle (harsh or late shifts)
c: Output wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Driver in the sending module unable to pull the line low

P2623.d: Engines with hydraulically actuated unit injectors (HEUI) fire their injectors with engine oil pressurised by a high-pressure pump; the injection pressure regulator (IPR) valve sets that oil rail pressure. P2623 says the PCM cannot drive the IPR because its circuit is open.
s: Engine cranks but does not start
Stalling or severe power loss
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Loose or corroded IPR connector, broken wire on the high-pressure pump cover
Faulty IPR driver in the PCM

P2624.d: P2624 is reserved for a control circuit of the injection pressure regulator that sits too low, typically a ground short on the line switched by the PCM. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hard start or no-start
Rough running, knocking or erratic power
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: IPR control wire chafed to ground near the valley or pump cover
Damaged driver stage in the PCM

P2625.d: With P2625 the module sees the injection pressure regulator circuit at too high a level: the switched line is shorted to battery voltage, or the IPR coil draws more current than the driver allows. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke summaries from 2003 to 2009 fold every IPR driver fault into P2623, and International's HEUI truck engines report through their own codes.
s: Long cranking or no-start
Low power, engine may stall
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: IPR control line shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
IPR coil with reduced resistance causing overcurrent
Faulty IPR driver in the PCM

P2626.d: Wide-band lambda probes such as the Bosch LSU 4.9 carry a calibration resistor in their plug; the engine module uses it to scale the pumping current. P2626 says this trim path at the front probe of bank 1 looks open.
s: Check engine light
Fuel control falls back to open loop on bank 1
Slightly higher fuel consumption or rough idle
c: Front wide-band probe defective (trim resistor, pump cell or heater damage)
Trim line broken or pin pushed back in the six-pin probe connector
Moisture or corrosion in the probe connector raising the measured resistance
Engine software requiring an update after probe replacement (some makes)

P2627.d: P2627 marks a trim signal below its plausible range at the first wide-band probe of bank 1. On Ford petrol engines with NTK probes the interface chip sets it when the resistor line (RL) is open or touches ground; Bosch-equipped Fords do not use it.
s: Check engine light
Further oxygen or NOx sensor codes stored at the same time
On diesels possibly boost or aftertreatment codes and reduced power
c: Trim/resistor line open or chafed to ground between probe and engine module
Wide-band probe or NOx sensor internally faulty
Loose or leaking charge-air ducts on diesel engines (GM L5P)

P2628.d: With P2628 the trim input of the front wide-band probe on bank 1 lies above its permitted range. Ford's 2020-23 petrol summary reserves it for NTK probes, where the interface chip reports the resistor line shorted to battery voltage.
s: Check engine light
Mixture control without probe feedback, higher consumption
On diesels NOx-related codes and possible SCR warnings
c: Trim line shorted to battery or another supply in the harness or plug
Wide-band probe or NOx sensor delivering an implausible value
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor drawing in outside air

P2629.d: P2629 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2626 and only exists on V or boxer engines with two front wide-band probes. The module finds the trim branch of that probe interrupted.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 fuel control without wide-band feedback
Possibly further bank 2 fuel trim codes
c: Bank 2 front probe faulty, including heater damage (Mercedes M278/M157)
Open trim wire or loose terminal at the bank 2 probe connector
Outdated engine software (update called for together with new probes)

P262A.d: Common-rail diesels learn how long each injector must be energised to deliver its tiny pilot shot. Ford's 6.7 L Power Stroke does this with Zero Fuel Calibration: during overrun with rail pressure set to 300 bar, one injector fires small test pulses and the resulting rise in crankshaft speed tells the module the real quantity; the learned offset then corrects every pilot injection of that injector.
s: Check engine light
Louder combustion knock, especially at idle and light load
Often no noticeable change in driveability
c: Driving pattern rarely offers long overrun phases in high gear (towing, city use)
Injector drift or wear so the test pulse does not give a usable response
Disturbed crankshaft speed or rail pressure signal
Non-original engine calibration interfering with the learning routine

P262B.d: P262B concerns the timer that keeps counting inside a control module while the vehicle is shut down, used to measure how long it has been off. GM runs two checks on it: a count-up test while run/crank is inactive, failing when two consecutive readings differ by over 1.5 s in 4 of 20 one-second samples, and a range test comparing the hardware timer with a mirror timer at shutdown or restart (deviation above 25 % in th
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Possibly other control module codes stored at the same time
c: Poor ECM power or ground connection, momentary supply loss
Ignition relay or its control circuit not supplying the module
Diagnostic calibration too sensitive to fast engine cool-down
Internal timer hardware fault in the control module

P262C.d: Engine modules supply groups of sensors from separately regulated 5 V outputs, lettered A, B, C and so on; G is the seventh such supply. P262C is the general fault of this output, typically an interruption so that the sensors behind it lose their feed and report signals near zero together.
s: Check engine light
Several sensor codes appearing at the same time
Reduced power or limp mode depending on the affected sensors
c: Broken reference wire or splice feeding the sensors of circuit G
Loose or corroded pin at the engine module or a sensor plug
Internal regulator of the engine module for output G failed

P262D.d: P262D says the 5 V reference output G of the engine module is being dragged below its lower limit. Usually something on the line conducts to ground: a chafed wire, water in a plug, or one sensor with an internal short loading the whole group.
s: Check engine light
Several sensors report low or invalid values together
Limp mode, reduced power or starting problems possible
c: Reference wire G chafed to ground or engine metal
One sensor on circuit G with internal short pulling the supply down
Water or corrosion in a connector of the group
Weak internal regulator of the engine module

P262E.d: With P262E the 5 V supply G that the engine module feeds to a sensor group sits above its upper limit. That points to an external voltage source getting onto the line, for example a reference wire rubbed through against a 12 V feed or a sensor signal wire, or to a regulator inside the module that no longer holds its setpoint.
s: Check engine light
Readings of several sensors too high or implausible
Limp mode or reduced power possible
c: Reference wire G shorted to a 12 V feed or another powered circuit
Sensor on the group feeding voltage back into the reference
Internal regulator of the engine module out of tolerance

P262F.d: P262F is the plausibility check of reference output G. The voltage is neither shorted nor missing, yet it wanders outside a tighter tolerance band or jumps around, which falsifies every ratiometric sensor on that circuit.
s: Check engine light
Sporadic implausible values from several sensors
Occasional hesitation or limp mode
c: Poor ground connection of the engine module
Loose pin or splice on circuit G opening briefly under vibration
Sensor on the group drawing excessive current
Drifting internal regulator of the engine module

P2630.d: P2630 reports a trim input that is too low at the upstream wide-band probe of bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. Ford's petrol summaries of 2020-23 set it only with NTK probes, where the sensor interface chip sees the resistor line open or grounded; the same chip check runs for about 10 s before a fault is stored.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 running in open loop
Fuel economy slightly worse
c: Resistor line of the bank 2 probe open or rubbed through to ground
Damaged or heat-affected connector near the exhaust

P2631.d: P2631 flags a trim value above the valid window for the first wide-band probe on bank 2. Ford assigns it to NTK probe installations: the interface chip notices the resistor line pulled up to battery voltage, as from a chafed wire touching a powered circuit.
s: Check engine light
Lambda control on bank 2 disabled
Possibly additional circuit codes from the same harness
c: Bank 2 resistor line shorted to a powered wire in the harness
Bank 2 front probe with internal short
Non-matching replacement probe or repaired connector without the original resistor

P2632.d: Fuel pump B is a second pump beside the main one: a transfer pump between two tanks, an in-line booster or a second in-tank pump. P2632 reports an open in its control circuit.
s: Fuel from the second tank is not transferred, gauge drops faster
Possible stalling when the main tank runs dry
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Failed transfer pump relay, fuse or relay socket
Open wire or corroded connector at the pump or tank
Pump motor or pump driver module open internally
Outdated scan tool cannot command the pump (GM PIT5212B)

P2633.d: P2633 is the ground-short code of the second fuel pump circuit. GM's 2014 LML diesel table checks the ground-switched relay output of the fuel transfer pump while it is off and flags 0.5 ohm or less between signal and ground, held for 3 s, as Type B.
s: Blown fuse, second pump does not run
Fuel not transferred from the auxiliary tank
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Chafed pump wire grounded against frame or tank strap
Water in the connector under the vehicle

P2634.d: P2634 indicates that the drive of the second fuel pump reads as shorted to battery voltage or carries too much current. For the 6.6 L LML with dual tanks, GM's 2014 table judges the transfer pump relay output while it is switched on and treats 0.5 ohm or less toward controller power, lasting 3 s, as a Type B fault.
s: Second pump runs constantly or is shut off by the module
Fuel level display between tanks inconsistent
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Worn or binding pump drawing excess current
Relay with shorted coil or stuck contacts

P2635.d: P2635 judges the main fuel pump by its result rather than its wiring: the module compares the measured fuel pressure with the commanded value and flags a pump that falls short or overshoots. GM's 2019 tables do this with filtered rail pressure error against calibrated low and high limits, with pump circuit and pressure sensor codes excluded first, and store it as Type B after two trips; the 2020 diesel table uses the
s: Hesitation, surging or loss of power under load
Hard starting or stalling
Whining noise from the fuel tank
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Worn or leaking in-tank pump module
Clogged filter or blocked pickup, e.g. gelled diesel in cold weather
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump or pump control module
Fuel pressure sensor reading wrong without its own code

P2636.d: P2636 is the flow check for fuel pump B, in practice mostly the transfer pump of trucks with two tanks. GM's 2014 table for the 6.6 L LML compares how fast the levels in both tanks fall while the pump runs; if they do not move as expected for 140 s, a Type B fault is stored.
s: Fuel gauge shows empty although the second tank holds fuel
Engine may stall when the main tank runs dry
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Weak transfer pump not moving enough fuel between tanks
Restricted transfer line or design-related flow limit (GM recall 17067)
Refuelling with engine or ignition on confuses the level-based check
Faulty fuel level sender in one of the tanks

P2637.d: Many automatic transmissions ask the engine to cut torque briefly during an upshift and then check whether the engine actually did so. P2637 is stored by the transmission controller when that feedback for request A shows the engine did not follow.
s: Check transmission lamp on
Harsh or too quick upshifts
Gear range limited
c: Engine control module calibration not following the torque reduction request
Transmission calibration not matched to the engine
J1939/CAN data link fault between engine and transmission

P2638.d: P2638 says the torque feedback for request A is present but its value does not fit the situation, for example an engine torque figure that drifts away from what the transmission expects during a shift. Honda documents it on its nine-speed automatic: on low-mileage 2016 Pilots the MIL lit and the gear indicator flashed because the idle learn had not been done properly before delivery, so the fix is a PCM reset with th
s: MIL on and gear position indicator flashing
Rough or delayed gear changes
c: Idle learn not completed after PCM reset or delivery
Outdated transmission software with oversensitive torque monitoring
Engine torque estimate skewed by air leaks or sensor errors

P2639.d: P2639 means the torque management feedback signal A stays below its valid range, so the transmission controller cannot read a usable torque confirmation from the engine. No manufacturer explains this exact code publicly.
s: Transmission warning or stored code
Firm or flared shifts
c: Engine and transmission software versions not matched
Torque feedback message missing or corrupted on the data bus
Hard-wired feedback line shorted to ground

P263A.d: P263A means the engine module has found the line that switches the malfunction indicator lamp shorted to ground. GM checks it while the low-side driver is off: if the voltage stays low with an impedance to ground of about 0.5 ohm, the lamp control is faulty; the 2014 tables need 50 of 63 samples at 50 ms intervals, the 2019 tables a single sample, with run/crank voltage of at least 11 V and remote start inactive.
s: Engine warning lamp lit permanently
Code stored even though the lamp cannot report it reliably
c: MIL control wire chafed and touching ground
Loss of ignition 1 voltage via main relay or fuse block terminal
Faulty lamp input in the instrument cluster

P263B.d: P263B is stored when the MIL control line is stuck at supply voltage while the module has switched its driver on to light the lamp. GM treats an impedance toward power of about 0.5 ohm as the fault and needs 4 failures within 5 samples, each 50 ms apart, provided run/crank voltage is at least 11 V and no remote start is running.
s: Engine warning lamp does not light, not even at key-on bulb check
Other emissions codes stored without warning
c: MIL control wire shorted to a positive feed
Ignition 1 supply interrupted at relay or fuse block
Lamp driver in the engine module failed

P263C.d: Modern diesel glow systems switch each plug through a semiconductor driver inside a glow plug control module (GPCM). P263C reports that such a driver does not behave as commanded.
s: Check engine light, glow indicator may flash
Hard or long cranking when cold
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
c: Output stage inside the glow plug control module failed
Glow plug or plug wire with short, overloading the driver
Poor GPCM power feed or ground causing erratic switching

P263D.d: DEF turns solid at about -11 °C, so SCR systems heat the tank, pump and lines electrically. P263D concerns the power stage that switches these heaters rather than a heater element.
s: Check engine light and DEF/SCR warning
DEF not thawing in cold weather, dosing delayed
Countdown to speed or power limitation possible
c: Heater power stage overheating from excessive load current
Partially shorted heater element or wiring drawing too much current
Internal fault of the module that drives the heaters

P263E.d: The first glow plug control module measures its own internal temperature and reports P263E when it runs too hot, since its power semiconductors carry tens of amps during glowing. GM's 6.6 L L5P Duramax tables set it at a module temperature above 123 °C while the plugs are commanded on and coolant is below 60 °C, type B.
s: Check engine light, glow lamp flashing
Glowing cut short, hard cold starts
White smoke after cold start
c: Defective glow plugs drawing excess current (e.g. Ram ProMaster plugs without O-ring)
Repeated start attempts or very long glow periods in severe cold
Internal fault or poor heat dissipation of the glow plug module

P263F.d: P263F is reserved for engines with a second glow plug control module, for instance one per cylinder bank on large V engines; it reports that this second unit has exceeded its permitted internal temperature. No manufacturer documents P263F publicly, and the documented North American V8 diesels from Ford and GM manage all eight plugs with a single module, so they only use the module 1 code P263E.
s: Check engine light, glow lamp flashing
Harder cold start, uneven running until warm
c: High-current or shorted glow plugs on the bank served by module 2
Long or repeated glow phases in severe cold
Internal fault or poor cooling of glow plug module 2

P2640.d: P2640 is the high-range fault of torque management feedback signal A: the confirmation that the transmission controller receives after asking the engine for a torque change carries a value above the plausible upper limit. On Allison-equipped trucks this feedback is not a separate wire but part of the engine data broadcast on the J1939 link, so a high reading usually means the engine claims more torque than is physica
s: Check transmission lamp or MIL on, depending on calibration
Firm or abrupt upshifts
Torque reduction during shifts no longer active
c: Engine ECM software reports torque values the transmission calibration does not accept
Outdated or wrong transmission controller calibration
Hard-wired feedback line shorted to voltage (where used)

P2641.d: On Allison automatics, feedback B belongs to Low Range Torque Protection (LRTP): in the low ranges the TCM caps engine torque to spare gears and output shaft and checks that the engine respects the cap. P2641 sets when the engine reports more torque than permitted.
s: CHECK TRANS lamp on
Low Reverse or other low ranges unavailable
Code appears under high load, often without noticeable drivability change
c: Engine ECM software below the level required for the transmission (Cummins, Mack, Volvo)
Engine broadcasts torque above the low-range limit requested by the TCM
Transmission calibration not matched to the engine

P2642.d: P2642 means feedback signal B arrives and lies inside its valid range, yet its value makes no sense for the current operating state, for example a torque figure that drifts away from what a limited request should produce or that changes implausibly fast. No manufacturer explains P2642 publicly.
s: Rough or delayed shifts
Transmission warning lamp on
Low ranges restricted
c: Engine and transmission software versions do not match
Idle or torque adaptation not learned after service
Faulty input to the engine torque model (air mass, intake air temperature)

P2643.d: With P2643 the transmission controller sees feedback signal B below its lower limit, so it cannot confirm that the engine is holding the torque level it asked for. No manufacturer describes this exact code in public documents.
s: Transmission warning lamp on
Low ranges or reverse low not selectable
Harsh shifts because torque reduction is missing
c: Torque message missing or sent with a default value on the data link
Bus or signal wiring damaged, short to ground

P2644.d: P2644 reports that torque management feedback B exceeds its upper range limit. No manufacturer publishes a code-specific description.
s: Transmission warning lamp on
Low ranges blocked
Shift quality reduced
c: Engine software sends torque with a scaling the transmission does not expect
Engine calibration older than the level required by the transmission maker
Wired feedback line shorted to voltage

P2645.d: Engines that switch valve lift or deactivate cylinders through their rocker arms use an actuator, usually an oil control solenoid, to send oil to the locking pins. P2645 means the engine controller sees the drive circuit of actuator A on bank 1 as open: the state it commands and the state it reads back on the line disagree.
s: MIL on, often on the first trip
No change to high lift, weak pull at high engine speed
Cylinder deactivation or economy mode no longer engages
c: Open coil in the rocker arm oil control solenoid
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked solenoid connector
Broken wire in the control or supply line
Faulty output driver in the engine control module

P2646.d: P2646 is a mechanical-hydraulic plausibility fault: actuator A on bank 1 was commanded to switch the rocker arms, yet the engine did not change lift, or responded too weakly. GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 tests this intrusively by toggling between high and low lift at 1,200 to 1,800 rpm and 40 to 230 Nm with warm oil (30 to 130 °C) and judges the resulting phaser oil-pressure ripple with a filtered average; it normally co
s: MIL on after a completed test drive
Engine feels flat above mid-range speed
Higher fuel consumption
c: Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Sticking spool or clogged screen in the oil control solenoid
Seized locking pin in the switching rocker arm
Faulty lift controller or outdated ECM calibration (Toyota Valvematic)

P2647.d: Here actuator A on bank 1 is believed to stay engaged: the rocker arms remain locked in the switched mode although the controller has asked for the default lift. GM's 2015 four-cylinder table 15OBDG05 detects this with the same intrusive lift toggle as P2646 but flags a filtered pressure-ripple value that falls below its limit; conditions are 1,200 to 1,800 rpm, 40 to 230 Nm, oil pressure 50 to 1,000 kPa, Type A afte
s: Rough or lumpy idle
Misfire at low load
Sluggish response when pulling away
c: Oil control solenoid leaks oil while switched off
Locking pin jammed in the engaged position
Faulty rocker arm oil pressure switch (Honda VTEC)

P2648.d: P2648 points to a low-side electrical fault on the control line of rocker arm actuator A, bank 1: the line reads low, typically a short to ground or a solenoid with shorted turns. GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 tests the driver for short-to-ground faults with ignition in crank or run and more than 11 V, trips after 100 bad samples out of 120 and lights the MIL at once (Type A).
s: MIL on immediately
No switching to the second lift stage
Reduced top-end power
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Shorted turns in the solenoid winding
Moisture or oil bridging pins in the connector

P2649.d: The counterpart to P2648: the control circuit of rocker arm actuator A on bank 1 reads high, which means a short to battery voltage or a driver that cannot pull the line down. In GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 the check needs the output driver commanded on, ignition in crank or run and supply above 11 V; 100 failures in 120 samples set a Type A fault.
s: MIL on immediately
Lift switching disabled or permanently active
Rough running at idle if the actuator stays energised
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Output driver in the engine controller no longer switches
Open ground side of the solenoid circuit

P264A.d: Some valve lift systems report back where the rocker arm actuator actually is, rather than relying on oil pressure; continuously variable designs driven by an electric motor, such as Toyota Valvematic, work this way. P264A is the general circuit fault for the position sensor of actuator A on bank 1: signal missing or implausible without a clear low or high pattern.
s: MIL on
Lift held at a fixed value, less power
Higher fuel consumption
c: Loose or corroded position sensor connector
Damaged signal, supply or ground wire

P264B.d: Range/Performance means the bank 1 feedback sensor for actuator A delivers a signal inside its electrical limits that still does not fit what the engine expects, for example a position that lags or overshoots the commanded one, or that fails to move when the actuator is driven. CARB requires valve lift systems to catch target errors and slow response before emissions exceed set limits.
s: MIL on after a drive cycle
Hesitation or uneven power delivery
Idle speed fluctuating
c: Sensor loose or misaligned on its mount

P264C.d: P264C is set when the signal from the position sensor of rocker arm actuator A, bank 1, sits below its valid window. Typical electrical explanations are a short of the signal wire to ground, a lost 5 V reference, or a sensor that has failed internally.
s: MIL on
Weaker pull, lift no longer varied
Higher fuel consumption

P264D.d: With P264D the position signal of actuator A on bank 1 reads above its plausible maximum. An open ground return, a signal line touching the 5 V or battery feed, or water in the connector can push it up.
s: MIL on
Engine runs on a fixed lift setting
Noticeably less power
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Water ingress in the sensor connector

P264E.d: P264E covers a feedback signal from the position sensor of actuator A, bank 1, that drops out or jumps for short moments rather than staying low or high. Loose terminals, a cracked wire flexing with engine movement, or interference on an unshielded line are the usual reasons, and the fault may vanish when the vehicle is parked.
s: MIL on, sometimes clearing by itself
Surging or hesitation
Uneven idle
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire cracked inside the insulation by engine movement
Electrical interference on the signal line

P264F.d: Some engine controllers store the serial number of the engine they belong to, much like the VIN. P264F is logged when that entry is empty or does not fit.
s: MIL on after control module replacement
Usually no change in how the engine runs
c: Engine serial number not written after PCM/ECM replacement
Serial number from another engine or used control module
Stored configuration lost through a memory fault in the module

P2650.d: Some engines split rocker arm switching into two stages or groups, each fed by its own oil control solenoid; the second one is called actuator B. P2650 is logged when the engine controller finds the drive line of that B solenoid on bank 1 open, so switching the output on or off brings no matching electrical response.
s: Check engine light on
Second switching stage never engages, less power or economy in that range
Possibly no other noticeable change in driving
c: Open winding in the B rocker arm oil control solenoid
Terminal pushed out or corroded in the solenoid B connector
Wire chafed through near the valve cover or harness clips
Failed output stage for solenoid B in the engine control module

P2651.d: In the generic definition, P2651 says the B stage of rocker arm switching on bank 1 did not engage when requested, or engaged too weakly to be confirmed. Controllers usually verify the change through an oil pressure switch in the rocker gallery or through a measurable shift in engine behaviour.
s: MIL on, sometimes only now and then
Engine lacks pull in the speed range served by stage B
Fault may not return right after clearing
c: Intermittently failing rocker arm oil pressure switch (Honda i-VTEC)
Oil level too low or oil of the wrong grade
Clogged filter screen or sticking spool in solenoid B
Locking pin in the switchable rocker arm seized by deposits

P2652.d: P2652 means the controller thinks stage B of the bank 1 rocker switching stays engaged after release was commanded, usually because the confirming oil pressure switch still signals pressure. Honda documents it in two ways.
s: MIL on, possibly together with P3400 on Honda V6
Rough or uneven running, especially at low load
Cylinder deactivation no longer works
c: Rocker arm oil pressure switch B reporting pressure permanently
Solenoid B lets oil through in its closed position
Locking pin stuck in the engaged position
Switch signal line shorted to voltage (Honda four-cylinder meaning)

P2653.d: P2653 points to a voltage that is too low on the control line of rocker arm solenoid B, bank 1. On a solenoid switched from the supply side, a line rubbing against the engine block or a shorted coil pulls the signal down while the output is active; the controller's driver then reports an overcurrent or a low-voltage state.
s: MIL on soon after the fault appears
B stage switched off, reduced power or economy
c: Control wire of solenoid B shorted to engine ground
Shorted turns inside the solenoid B coil
Engine oil inside the connector creating a leakage path

P2654.d: P2654 reports a voltage that is too high on the wire that drives rocker solenoid B, bank 1, typically when the line touches a battery-fed wire or the driver's ground side is bridged. With a ground-switched solenoid, that kind of short can energise the valve permanently, so the B stage may stay engaged regardless of the command, which the engine feels as rough idle or misfire at low speed.
s: MIL on
Rough idle or misfire if the B stage stays engaged
Possible blown fuse on the solenoid supply
c: Solenoid B control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Internal short in solenoid B lowering its resistance
Shorted output transistor in the engine control module

P2655.d: P2655 is the bank 2 twin of P2645: on a V or boxer engine with a separate rocker arm actuator per cylinder bank, the drive circuit of actuator A on the side without cylinder 1 is open, so the state the controller sets and the state it sees on the wire differ. No manufacturer documents P2655 publicly.
s: MIL on
Banks run unevenly, slight roughness
Reduced power or economy
c: Broken wire in the harness to the bank 2 solenoid
Terminal pushed out of the connector housing
Open coil in the bank 2 oil control solenoid

P2656.d: For bank 2, P2656 reports that actuator A was told to switch the rocker arms but the expected change in valve lift did not show up, or it was too small. Since such engines give every bank a separate oil feed and solenoid, a clogged screen or sticking spool on that side alone is enough.
s: MIL on after a completed test
Weaker response at higher engine speed
Higher fuel consumption
c: Low, wrong or sludged engine oil
Clogged oil screen or sticking spool at the bank 2 solenoid
Seized locking pin in a bank 2 rocker arm

P2657.d: P2657 is the stuck-on case for bank 2: actuator A keeps the rocker arms of the second bank in their switched mode after the controller has asked for the base setting. On a cylinder deactivation design that could mean valves stay closed on that side; on a two-step design the high-lift profile stays active at idle.
s: Misfire codes on bank 2 cylinders
Lumpy idle
Poor low-speed driveability
c: Bank 2 solenoid passing oil while switched off
Locking pin stuck in the engaged position
Debris in the bank 2 oil passage

P2658.d: P2658 flags the bank 2 control line of rocker arm actuator A as too low, the classic sign of a short to ground or a coil with damaged windings. The test is purely electrical and runs whenever the controller drives the output, regardless of oil condition.
s: MIL on immediately
Lift switching disabled
Less power or higher consumption
c: Bank 2 control wire shorted to ground
Damaged winding in the bank 2 solenoid
Harness insulation damaged by exhaust heat

P2659.d: P2659 covers the bank 2 control circuit of actuator A reading high: the wire is shorted to a voltage source or the controller's driver stage no longer switches it to ground. No manufacturer documents P2659 publicly.
s: MIL on immediately
Bank 2 lift stays switched or switching is disabled
Rough idle in some cases
c: Bank 2 control wire shorted to a voltage source
Controller output stage no longer switching to ground
Neighbouring pins bridged in the connector

P265A.d: Lift systems that move the rocker geometry with an electric motor, such as Toyota Valvematic, need a sensor that tells the engine controller the actual adjustment angle. P265A flags a general electrical problem with the feedback sensor that reports where actuator B on bank 1 sits: the controller sees no usable signal but cannot classify it as simply too low or too high.
s: MIL on
Lift held at a fixed value, sluggish response
Higher fuel consumption
c: Loose or corroded connector at the B position sensor
Open 5 V reference or sensor ground wire
Failed position sensor inside the lift controller

P265B.d: Toyota documents this code on Valvematic engines, where an electric lift controller turns a shaft that alters rocker geometry and reports its angle back. P265B is set when that feedback stays electrically valid but does not track the target.
s: MIL on, often together with P2646
Reduced power and slower throttle response
Fault may return after a short rev to 3,500 rpm
c: Continuously variable lift controller sticking or worn
Stored learn values no longer match the mechanism
Drifting angle sensor in the controller

P265C.d: The angle or position sensor of rocker arm actuator B, bank 1, normally works inside a voltage band that never touches the lower rail. If the reading falls below that band, the engine controller logs P265C, because a value near zero cannot correspond to any real actuator position.
s: MIL on
Engine runs with fixed lift, less power
c: Sensor B signal wire grounded through damaged insulation
Internal fault in position sensor B

P265D.d: P265D stands for a feedback signal from position sensor B, bank 1, that sits above its valid ceiling. A reading pinned near the supply voltage usually means the signal is no longer pulled toward a real value: the sensor ground has opened, the signal wire touches a reference or battery line, or moisture has bridged pins in the plug.
s: MIL on
Lift frozen at default, weaker acceleration
c: Open ground wire of position sensor B
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the sensor plug

P265E.d: Here the bank 1 position signal for actuator B is neither stuck low nor high; instead it jumps, flickers or briefly vanishes faster than the mechanism could physically move. The engine controller compares successive readings and flags P265E when the rate of change or the number of dropouts exceeds what a motor-driven lift mechanism can produce.
s: MIL on and off over several trips
Surging or uneven power delivery
c: Fretting corrosion on sensor B terminals
Conductor broken inside its insulation, opening under vibration
Interference from ignition or other high-current wiring

P265F.d: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their output through an electric control valve on the back of the compressor housing. On Ford's externally controlled design the PCM drives that valve with a pulse-width signal and aims for an evaporator temperature of roughly 3 to 8 °C; Volkswagen calls the part regulator valve N280, a coil of around 10 ohms.
s: A/C cools weakly or inconsistently
Compressor runs at fixed or minimum output
c: Control valve sticking or internally worn
Refrigerant charge too low, so pressures do not follow the valve command
Corroded connector or high resistance in the valve circuit

P2660.d: P2660 concerns V-type or boxer engines with switchable rocker arms on both cylinder banks: the controller sees the drive circuit of solenoid B on bank 2, the side without cylinder 1, as broken. An open coil, a disconnected plug after valve cover work, or a cut wire leaves the output without load, so the command and the electrical feedback disagree.
s: MIL on
Bank 2 B stage inactive, uneven running between banks possible
c: Solenoid B plug on bank 2 left unplugged or not latched after repairs
Open coil in bank 2 solenoid B
Cut or broken wire on the bank 2 harness branch

P2661.d: P2661 is the functional check of rocker arm stage B on bank 2: although the solenoid circuit is electrically sound, the commanded switch did not happen or the confirmation (an oil pressure switch reading or a change in cam phaser or engine response) stayed too small. Bank 2 means the engine has two cylinder heads, so the fault concerns only half of the cylinders, which may show as a difference between the banks.
s: MIL after a completed drive cycle
Less power in the range where stage B should engage
Higher fuel consumption
c: Low oil level or poor oil supply to the bank 2 head
Partly blocked oil gallery or screen on bank 2
Sticking solenoid spool or seized locking pins on bank 2

P2662.d: With P2662 the controller concludes that stage B on bank 2 stays switched after it has requested the default mode. Detection depends on the design: a pressure switch that keeps indicating oil pressure, or engine behaviour on that bank that still matches the engaged state.
s: MIL on
Uneven idle or misfire on bank 2, worse when cold
c: Bank 2 solenoid B seeping oil when closed
Blocked drain path keeping oil pressure on the rockers
Locking pins jammed in the coupled position by debris or wear

P2663.d: P2663 is stored when the control line to solenoid B on bank 2 reads too low, most often a short to ground somewhere between the module and the second cylinder head. On V engines that harness branch often runs along the back of the block or under the intake manifold, where heat and vibration wear through insulation.
s: MIL on
Stage B on bank 2 out of action, power or economy reduced
c: Bank 2 control wire worn through and touching ground
Bank 2 solenoid B coil with collapsed resistance
Faulty output driver for bank 2 solenoid B

P2664.d: P2664 signals excessive voltage on the control line of solenoid B, bank 2. Contact with a powered conductor, for example where several solenoid and injector feeds share a connector, or a driver that can no longer pull the line down, are the typical causes.
s: MIL on
Misfire or rough idle on bank 2 if the stage stays engaged
c: Short to a powered feed inside a shared engine connector
Output driver in the control module stuck off
Internally shorted solenoid B on bank 2

P2665.d: Engines that can burn a second fuel such as compressed natural gas use electric shut-off valves to keep that fuel locked in when it is not wanted. GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel has two of them, both normally closed: a high-pressure cut-off at the tank and a low-pressure cut-off at the regulator, which the ECM energises only in CNG mode while the engine cranks or runs.
s: Engine runs only on gasoline, gas mode not available
Fuel mode lamp flashes or shows an error
c: Loose or corroded connector at the valve (often exposed under the vehicle)
Broken wire in the control circuit

P2666.d: P2666 is stored when the control line of fuel shut-off valve B sits at too low a voltage, the typical sign of a short to ground between module and valve or inside the coil. Depending on how the driver is built, the valve may then open whenever the ignition is on, or the module switches the output off for protection.
s: Gas mode switched off, engine runs on gasoline
Fuel mode lamp flashes rapidly
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water ingress in the valve connector

P2667.d: With P2667 the module measures excess voltage on the wire that drives shut-off valve B, usually because the wire touches a supply circuit. Safety matters here: on a low-side driven valve a short to voltage can keep the coil energised even when the module wants the valve closed, so the gaseous fuel may not be shut off reliably.
s: Gas mode disabled, operation on gasoline only
Fuel mode lamp indicates an error
Possible gas smell if the valve does not close
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage supply
Corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Faulty output stage in the control module

P2668.d: Bi-fuel vehicles tell the driver which fuel is in use through a small indicator, often built into the fuel selector button. On GM's 2016 Silverado and Sierra with CNG the light is off on gasoline, steady on natural gas, flashes once per second during a changeover and flashes about ten times per second when the CNG system has a fault; the 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel uses a similar light in its CNG switch.
s: Fuel mode lamp stays dark in gas mode
No flashing during fuel changeover or on errors
c: Indicator LED or bulb in the selector switch failed
Open wire or loose connector at the switch
Lamp driver in the control module defective

P2669.d: Many transmission controllers feed their solenoids through internal high-side switches, called actuator supply A and B. Ford's 6R140 splits its Transmission Solenoid Power Control into two wires: TSPC-A powers shift solenoids A, C and E (fault P0657), TSPC-B powers SSB, SSD, TCC and line pressure control (P2669).
s: Transmission stuck in a fixed gear (failsafe)
Harsh engagements due to maximum line pressure
MIL or transmission warning on
c: Open supply wire or connector between module and transmission bulkhead
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
High-side switch inside the controller failed

P266A.d: P266A is the basic circuit fault for the bank 2 position sensor of rocker arm actuator A. It only applies to engines that have a lift actuator with position feedback on each cylinder bank, which is rare; most switching rocker systems on V engines rely on oil pressure switches or none at all.
s: MIL on
Lift on bank 2 no longer adjusted
Reduced power and smoothness
c: Poor contact at the bank 2 sensor connector
Damaged wiring between sensor and engine controller

P266B.d: For bank 2, P266B means the position reported for actuator A is electrically valid but does not match what was commanded or changes too slowly. CARB expects variable lift monitors to notice when the commanded position is missed or reached too late, and a sensor whose reading drifts from the real actuator position defeats both.
s: MIL on after a drive cycle
Uneven running between the banks
Hesitation under load
c: Sensor reading drifting from the true position
Control software calling for an update

P266C.d: P266C reports a bank 2 position sensor signal for actuator A that has fallen under its lower plausibility limit. Grounded signal wires, a missing sensor supply or an internal sensor short pull it down; a connector left half unplugged after other work on the harder-to-reach side of the engine is another possible trigger.
s: MIL on
Bank 2 held at fixed lift
Less pulling power
c: Bank 2 sensor signal shorted to ground
Connector not fully seated after other repairs

P266D.d: P266D is logged when the bank 2 position feedback of rocker arm actuator A climbs above its upper limit. Typical reasons are an interrupted sensor ground, a signal wire chafed through onto a supply line, or corrosion that raises resistance.
s: MIL on
Lift on bank 2 frozen
Reduced power
c: Interrupted ground of the bank 2 sensor
Signal wire chafed onto a supply line

P266E.d: P266E describes a bank 2 position signal from actuator A that flickers: brief dropouts or spikes appear while the reading is otherwise fine. Heat cycling near the exhaust side, vibration on a loose pin or a harness rubbing on a bracket can produce it, and it often comes and goes.
s: MIL comes and goes
Hesitation or uneven running
Fault often not present at the workshop
c: Connector contact degraded by heat cycling near the exhaust
Loose pin vibrating in the bank 2 sensor plug

P266F.d: Refrigerant distribution valve A is a solenoid that opens or closes one branch of the A/C circuit, for instance a rear evaporator or a battery chiller. Its driver stage in the control module protects itself: when the output current rises above its limit or the chip overheats, it switches off and reports P266F.
s: One A/C zone or the battery cooling stays inactive
Fault may return after cooling down
c: Valve coil with shorted turns drawing excessive current
Short in the valve harness or connector
Valve mechanically stuck so the coil stays loaded
Overheated or defective driver stage in the control module

P2670.d: P2670 is set when the second high-side actuator supply delivers too little voltage while it is switched on, which nearly always means a short to ground somewhere on the supply line or in a load connected to it. GM documents it in several controllers.
s: Failsafe gear, no normal shifting
MIL on immediately
Further solenoid circuit codes stored alongside
c: Supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted solenoid on the supplied group pulling the line down
Faulty high-side driver in the controller

P2671.d: P2671 points to voltage on the second actuator supply when the controller has switched it off, so the line is fed from outside or the switch inside the module no longer opens. The solenoids on that supply can then no longer be de-energised as a group, which defeats the failsafe.
s: Warning lamp after the next start
Often no immediate shift complaint
Failsafe may not engage correctly if another fault occurs
c: Supply line shorted to another powered circuit
High-side switch in the controller stuck closed
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the transmission connector

P2672.d: On diesels with an electronically controlled rotary or distributor pump, the controller needs to know how far the pump's actual delivery start sits from its nominal position relative to the crankshaft. P2672 flags that this stored or measured offset is wrong or outside the window the software accepts.
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or rough idle
Diesel knock, smoke or reduced power
c: Injection pump fitted or re-timed incorrectly after repair
Faulty pump timing or crank/cam reference signal
Worn pump drive (gear, belt, coupling) shifting the timing
Engine control software fault or wrong calibration

P2673.d: This code says the engine controller holds no valid learned value for the start of delivery of its injection pump. Such a value is usually taught after the pump or the controller is replaced, or after a software reflash, and lets the controller correct the pump's individual timing tolerance.
s: Check engine light on
Slightly rough running or more noise
c: Timing relearn skipped after pump or controller replacement
Software update interrupted or learned values lost
Relearn aborted because enable conditions (temperature, voltage) were not met

P2674.d: Electronically governed diesel injection pumps meter the quantity per stroke themselves, and each unit differs slightly in how much it delivers for a given command. P2674 reports that the quantity correction for the installed pump has not been learned or stored in the controller.
s: Check engine light on
Smoke or uneven idle
Reduced power
c: Quantity learn not run after pump or controller replacement
Pump calibration data missing, wrong or not matching the installed pump
Fuel metering actuator fault preventing the learn from completing

P2675.d: Some engines can change where the air cleaner draws its air, for example switching between a cold inlet at the front and a second opening in the engine bay, with a flap or valve moved by a solenoid or small motor. P2675 is the open or general circuit fault of this control: the module driving the flap detects that its output line carries no current or reports a fault it cannot classify further.
s: Warning light or stored code, often without MIL
Inlet flap no longer switches
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Connector at the inlet flap actuator loose or unplugged, often after air filter service
Broken wire in the actuator circuit
Open coil or motor winding in the flap actuator

P2676.d: P2676 means the control line of the air cleaner inlet flap sits at too low a voltage for the state the controller has commanded. On a low-side driven solenoid this typically appears when the line is shorted to ground and the actuator is energised permanently; on other designs a shorted coil pulls the voltage down.
s: Code stored, often without warning lamp
Inlet flap stuck in one position
Possibly changed intake noise
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the inlet flap actuator

P2677.d: The counterpart to P2676: the controller sees the drive line of the air cleaner inlet flap at too high a voltage, so it cannot pull the actuator in when asked. A short from the control wire to battery voltage, a failed output stage, or an open coil that leaves the line at supply level produce this pattern.
s: Code stored, often without warning lamp
Inlet flap remains in its default position
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open coil in the flap actuator
Failed output stage in the control module

P2678.d: In a sealed cooling system, air and vapour bubbles are carried through a thin vent line into the expansion tank, where they separate from the liquid; a bubble-free circuit avoids local hot spots, as cooling suppliers such as MAHLE point out. Some engines put an electrically switched valve in this degassing path so the controller can close it, for example to speed up warm-up.
s: Check engine light or stored code
Longer warm-up or slow heater output
Gurgling or air in the cooling system
c: Unplugged connector or broken wire to the degassing valve
Open solenoid coil in the degassing valve
Faulty driver in the control module

P2679.d: P2679 indicates that the control line of the switched valve in the coolant vent path to the expansion tank reads too low. Usually the wire is grounded somewhere, or the solenoid has shorted turns; with a low-side driver the valve may then stay energised regardless of the command.
s: Check engine light or stored code
Slow warm-up
Coolant level fluctuations in the expansion tank
c: Shorted turns in the degassing valve solenoid
Coolant or water leaking into the valve connector

P267A.d: Continuously variable lift systems turn a control or eccentric shaft with an electric motor and report the shaft angle back to the engine controller. On V engines each cylinder bank has its own mechanism; Nissan's VVEL on the VQ37VHR V6 and VK50VE V8 is an example of such a two-bank layout.
s: Check engine light on
Variable lift on bank 2 held at a fixed default
Reduced power or rough idle
c: Loose, corroded or damaged plug at the bank 2 position sensor
Broken or chafed signal, reference or ground wire
Internal fault of position sensor B, bank 2
Fault in the engine or lift control module input

P267B.d: P267B concerns the bank 2 feedback of lift actuator B when the signal is electrically sound but the angle it reports does not follow the commanded value, moves too slowly, or contradicts the mechanism's known travel. Faulty learning of the end stops, a slipping sensor mount, wear in the shaft drive or a sticking actuator can all produce this picture.
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation or reduced power
Uneven idle when lift is frozen on one bank
c: End-stop learn values lost or wrong after repair or battery disconnect
Worn or sticking shaft drive of actuator B on bank 2
Position sensor drifting or loose in its mount
Lift control software needing an update

P267C.d: With P267C the engine controller reads the bank 2 position signal of lift actuator B below its lowest valid value. A sensor of this kind is designed so that even the end stop of the shaft keeps a margin to zero volts, so a reading near ground points to an electrical cause: the signal line shorted to chassis, a lost 5 V reference, or a sensor with an internal short.
s: Check engine light on
Lift on bank 2 fixed at a default position
Noticeably weaker acceleration
c: Signal wire shorted to ground through damaged insulation
5 V reference supply to the sensor missing
Internal short in position sensor B, bank 2

P267D.d: P267D is stored when the angle feedback of lift actuator B on bank 2 rises above its upper valid limit. Typical causes are an open sensor ground, which lets the signal float toward the reference, a signal conductor touching a supply line, or water bridging contacts in the connector.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power with lift fixed on bank 2
Slightly higher fuel consumption
c: Open or high-resistance ground of the position sensor
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor plug

P267E.d: Here the bank 2 angle signal of lift actuator B is mostly plausible, yet it drops out for moments or jumps by amounts the motor-driven shaft could not cover in the time between two readings. The engine controller counts such events and sets P267E once they exceed its tolerance.
s: Check engine light that may come and go
Brief hesitation or surging
Uneven running when lift control on bank 2 hunts
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Wire broken inside insulation, opening under heat or vibration
Interference from nearby ignition or actuator wiring

P267F.d: Many control modules carry a temperature sensor on their own circuit board to protect output stages and, in transmission units, to back up fluid temperature. P267F adds an intermittent or erratic variant to the established family P0666 to P0669: the reading flickers, jumps or drops out briefly instead of being permanently too low, too high or implausible.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light
Harsh or delayed shifts if the module uses substitute values
Often no noticeable symptom
c: Internal defect of the control module or its temperature sensor
Unstable module supply or ground causing erratic readings
Module software misinterpreting the sensor signal

P2680.d: P2680 is the high-voltage fault of the degassing valve drive: the controller cannot pull the line down, so the valve stays in its unpowered state whatever is commanded. A wire touching a battery feed, an internally open solenoid, or a defective output transistor are the classic reasons.
s: Check engine light or stored code
Air pockets, gurgling or weak cabin heat
Temperature gauge higher than usual
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed
Internally open solenoid of the degassing valve
Defective output stage in the control module

P2681.d: Bypass valve A is an electrically driven coolant valve whose role differs by maker. P2681 flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit.
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up of engine or transmission
Maintenance or temperature warning message
c: Failed bypass valve (motor, gear or electronics)
Chafed harness or open fuse in the valve supply
Engine control software causing false detection

P2682.d: P2682 narrows the drive fault of bypass valve A to the low side: the output is pulled toward ground when it should not be. In GM's 2016 table for the second-generation Volt, the VICM sets it when motor driver 1 reports a short to low while the valve is commanded to the low position, with 4 failures in 5 samples and Type B.
s: Check engine light on
Weak cabin heat or slow warm-up
Possible overheating warning under load
c: Drive wire to the valve motor shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve motor or electronics
Coolant or water corrosion in the valve plug

P2683.d: For P2683 the drive of bypass valve A is shorted toward supply voltage or draws too much current. GM's 2016 Volt table has the VICM evaluate a short-to-high report from motor driver 1 while the valve is stopped or commanded to the high position; 16 failures out of 20 samples at 100 ms give a Type B fault.
s: Check engine light on
Changed heater output or warm-up time
Temperature warning in severe cases
c: Jammed valve or shorted valve motor drawing excess current
Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty motor driver in the control module

P2684.d: Some transmission controllers power groups of solenoids through several internal high-side outputs; supply C is the third of these rails, after A (P0657) and B (P2669). P2684 reports an open load on it.
s: Transmission in default gear or limp mode
MIL on after restart
Several solenoid circuit codes stored together
c: Broken wire or loose terminal between the module output and the supplied solenoids
Corroded or unseated transmission connector or internal lead frame
High-side output inside the controller defective

P2685.d: P2685 means the third actuator supply rail sags while it is switched on, almost always because the line or one of the loads it feeds has a path to ground. Unlike the open and switch faults of this rail, GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables check this one continuously during operation: if the voltage at high-side output 7 falls below a share of the supply, or the averaged output current runs too high, a timer counts up and t
s: MIL on during the same trip
Failsafe gear, no normal shifting
Blown fuse possible on the transmission supply
c: Supply wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted solenoid coil on this rail drawing excess current
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the whole supply down

P2686.d: The high case of supply C concerns voltage that should not be there: the rail stays live although the controller has turned it off. Causes are an internal high-side switch that no longer opens or an outside wire touching battery positive.
s: MIL after a second trip with the fault
Limp mode or fixed gear after restart
Code returns after clearing once the key has been off
c: Internal high-side switch of the controller stuck conducting
Supply wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit in the harness
Moisture in the transmission connector creating a leakage path

P2687.d: Diesel engines warm the fuel at the filter so that wax crystals do not block it in frost. P2687 says the control line of that heater is open.
s: Hard starting or stalling in severe cold
Power loss from a waxed fuel filter
Often no warning lamp, depending on model year
c: Heater relay coil open or relay not seated
Broken control wire or corroded terminal at the filter housing
Heater element open where it is switched directly without a relay

P2688.d: With P2688 the heater control line reads too low while the driver is off, which points to a grounded wire: the relay would then be energized all the time, and the filter heater runs even in summer and drains the battery after shutdown. GM's 2020 diesel table requires 0.5 ohm or less to ground and counts 10 failures in 20 samples taken every 100 ms; the code is Type C but, unlike its siblings, triggers a service-vehic
s: Service message or MIL, depending on model year
Battery drained after the vehicle stands
Fuel heater running constantly
c: Control wire chafed against the engine or frame and grounded
Water or fuel in the filter-housing connector

P2689.d: P2689 is logged when the fuel heater control line stays high even though the controller has commanded it on, so the relay coil is fed from battery positive and cannot be pulled in; the heater never works. GM's diesel ECM checks the low-side driver in its on state and treats 0.5 ohm or less to power as a short; the 2020 table uses 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms and Type C without lamp or message, while the 2014 table sets
s: No fuel heating, gelling risk below freezing
