Hard cold starts and rough idle until warm
Warning lamp only on some model years
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire
Heater relay sticking so feedback no longer matches the command
Low-side driver in the engine controller defective

P268A.d: P268A covers injector correction that relies on a learn routine rather than a printed code. GM's diesel tables 17OBDG04 to 19OBDG04A set it, Type A in one trip, when the small quantity learning (SQL) routine was not completed and stored before the vehicle left the assembly line.
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle or louder combustion noise
Often no noticeable change in driving
c: Injector quantity learn not completed after injector or controller replacement
Engine control software fault (e.g. Audi 2.0 TFSI 2025–2026)
Rail pressure deviation preventing correct learning
Injector worn beyond the correction range

P268B.d: Common rail and direct-injection petrol systems use a high pressure pump whose delivery is trimmed by a metering or volume control valve. Where the pump comes with individual correction data, or the controller has to learn its behaviour, P268B reports that this data is missing or was never taught.
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking or hard start
Reduced power with rail pressure deviations
c: Pump correction data not entered after pump replacement
Controller replaced or reflashed without transferring pump data
Pump variant does not match the software

P268C.d: Every modern diesel injector carries a correction code from the factory flow test, and the controller must hold the code of the injector in cylinder 1. P268C sets when that code is missing, outside its range or fails the checksum.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running or knock from cylinder 1
c: Correction code of a new cylinder 1 injector not entered
Code entered with a typing error, so the checksum fails
Controller replaced without transferring injector codes

P268D.d: P268D concerns the stored flow correction for the injector in cylinder 2. In GM's 2016 four-cylinder diesel table (16OBDG04) the test runs with ignition on and passes once the end-of-line injector adjustment (EIA) value has been written via DID $61; a missing value only counts as a failure when the manufacturer enable counter is zero, i.e.
s: Check engine light on
Slight misfire feel or noise from cylinder 2
c: Adjustment value of the cylinder 2 injector not programmed after replacement
Injectors moved between cylinders without updating codes
Programming session aborted (voltage drop, communication loss)

P268E.d: For cylinder 3 the controller compares the injector's correction value with what its software accepts. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary explains the idea well: each injector's code, kept in EEPROM, describes how far that unit departs from an idealised mean part, and a DTC is logged if the value is absent, out of range or its checksum is wrong.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driveability change
c: Cylinder 3 injector replaced, code not programmed
Code from an injector variant the software does not accept
Stored injector data corrupted in the controller

P268F.d: P268F flags missing or unusable correction data for the injector in cylinder 4. On four-cylinder diesels it closes the series: GM's 2014 table 14OBDG04 and 2016 table 16OBDG04 list P268C to P268F and nothing beyond.
s: Check engine light on
Possible rough idle or higher combustion noise
c: New cylinder 4 injector fitted without code programming
Code typed incorrectly into the scan tool
Used or replacement controller carrying another engine's codes

P2690.d: P2690 is the first code of the series that a four-cylinder engine cannot set; it needs at least five cylinders. It reports that the flow correction for the cylinder 5 injector is absent or rejected by the controller.
s: Check engine light on
Rarely uneven running
c: Cylinder 5 injector replaced without entering its code
Code entered for the wrong cylinder because of the bank numbering

P2691.d: P2691 refers to the injector in cylinder 6. For six-cylinder diesels it is the last of the per-cylinder codes: GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B stops at P2691, while the V8 table 25OBDG04A goes on to P2693.
s: Check engine light on
Possible knock or smoke from the affected cylinder
c: Cylinder 6 injector code missing after replacement
Entered value rejected as implausible by the software
Controller memory fault losing stored injector data

P2692.d: Only engines with seven or more cylinders can log P2692, which in practice means V8 diesels. It tells that the correction code for the cylinder 7 injector has not been stored or is unusable.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no drivability change
c: Injector in cylinder 7 replaced, code not programmed
Replacement controller without the vehicle's injector codes
Software variant for the wrong engine configuration

P2693.d: P2693 completes the series on V8 engines and covers the injector in cylinder 8. It is set when the controller finds no valid flow correction code for that position.
s: Check engine light on
Possible rough idle or knock
c: Code of the new cylinder 8 injector not entered
New or reset controller lacking all injector codes
Typing error in the cylinder 8 code

P2694.d: P2694 would flag bad or missing correction data for the injector in cylinder 9 and therefore only fits engines with nine or more cylinders, in road vehicles essentially V10s. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
c: Cylinder 9 injector code not programmed (ten-cylinder engines)
Scan tool decoding error on engines without a ninth cylinder
Controller software for a different engine

P2695.d: P2695 is reserved for the injector in cylinder 10, the highest cylinder number the J2012 series provides with its own data code. A ten-cylinder engine with individually coded injectors would be needed to set it, and none of the public OBD summaries reviewed here contains it: GM's 2025 V8 diesel table 25OBDG04A and Ford's 2023 diesel summary both stop at cylinder 8.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
c: Cylinder 10 injector code missing on a ten-cylinder engine
Misread code on engines with fewer cylinders

P2696.d: P2696 is the collective version of P268C–P2695: the controller rejects stored injector correction data without naming a cylinder. That suits systems that check the data block as a whole, or engines with more than ten cylinders.
s: Check engine light on
Louder engine noise or rough running
c: Injector codes lost during a software update or controller replacement
Injector replaced without programming its code
Corrupted injector data block in the controller

P2697.d: Many heavy diesels do not raise exhaust temperature for filter regeneration by late in-cylinder injection, but spray diesel straight into the exhaust ahead of the oxidation catalyst through a separate doser, often called the seventh injector. P2697 means the solenoid that meters this fuel cannot be driven because its circuit is open.
s: Active particulate filter regeneration not possible
Rising soot load, later derate
MIL on
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the dosing module
Harness to the dosing valve broken by heat or vibration
Dosing valve coil inside the module burnt open

P2698.d: P2698 is not about wiring but about whether the exhaust fuel doser does what it is told; most often the check looks for leakage when no dosing is requested. Ford's 3.2 L Transit (2017 and 2018 summaries) compares a measured temperature downstream of the injection point with a model after at least 6 h engine-off.
s: MIL on, often without noticeable drivability change
Regenerations fail or take unusually long
Higher fuel use or white exhaust smoke
c: Doser valve or nozzle leaking fuel into the exhaust
Coked nozzle or line causing low flow
Exhaust temperature sensor drifting and skewing the model comparison
Engine software needing the manufacturer update

P2699.d: P2699 flags the drive circuit of the exhaust fuel doser as too low, usually a grounded control wire or a shorted valve coil. The difference to P2697 matters in practice: an open circuit simply stops dosing, while a grounded line can switch the valve on without command if the short sits behind the driver, so raw fuel may reach a cold catalyst.
s: MIL on and regeneration inhibited
Possible white smoke if the valve opens uncommanded
Derate after prolonged soot build-up
c: Doser control wire grounded against the frame or exhaust bracket
Shorted coil of the dosing valve
Fuel or water inside the module connector

P269A.d: The high variant of the exhaust doser circuit means the control line shows supply voltage where the driver expects it to be pulled down, typically a short to battery positive or a driver that no longer conducts. In that state the valve cannot be opened, and a hard short can also overload the output, which the controller then switches off for protection.
s: MIL on, regeneration requests fail
Filter soot level climbs over time
Derate in later stages
c: Doser control wire shorted to a positive supply
Output stage in the controller not switching
Pin damage in the dosing module connector

P269B.d: Some diesels inject fuel into the exhaust through a small vaporizer whose glow plug turns the fuel into vapor before it reaches the oxidation catalyst. Ford calls this downstream injection (DSI) on the 3.2 L Transit, used so that filter regeneration needs fewer in-cylinder post injections and less oil is diluted.
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regenerations fail or become rare
More frequent in-cylinder regeneration, oil level may rise
c: Open wire or connector between engine computer and glow plug relay
Vaporizer glow plug relay coil open
Blown fuse in the glow plug control feed

P269C.d: P269C is the plausibility counterpart to the electrical control codes: the wires test fine, yet the control stage of the exhaust glow plug does not behave as commanded, for example a relay or driver that does not report the expected state or reacts too slowly. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regeneration incomplete
c: Glow plug relay switching late or not at all
Faulty feedback signal from the relay or driver
Low system voltage during the control check

P269D.d: A low reading on the exhaust glow plug control line points to a path to ground before the load, so the control stage cannot set the right level and the vaporizer glow plug may be switched wrongly. Ford is the documented user: in its 2017 and 2018 diesel summaries the 3.2 L Transit judges the downstream injection glow plug circuit by voltage windows, and a reading held between 1.95 and 2.175 V for 5 s is classed as a
s: MIL on
Regeneration suspended, rising soot load
Possible blown fuse in the glow plug feed
c: Control wire chafed on the exhaust or body and grounded
Shorted coil in the glow plug relay

P269E.d: When the exhaust glow plug control circuit reads close to battery voltage at the wrong moment, the control side has contact with a positive feed or the switching stage hangs open, so the vaporizer glow plug may stay energized or ignore commands. On Ford's 3.2 L Transit diesel the 2017 and 2018 summaries set P269E once the circuit holds between 10.9 and 12.32 V for 5 s with the ignition on.
s: MIL on
Glow plug failing early from constant heating
Regeneration curtailed
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Relay contacts welded, glow plug permanently powered
Output stage in the engine computer defective

P269F.d: While P269B concerns the line that commands the exhaust glow plug, P269F targets the load circuit itself: the heating element or its power feed is open, so no current flows even when the control stage switches correctly. A burnt-out element is the usual reason, followed by a loose terminal at the plug in the hot exhaust area.
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regenerations fail
c: Loose or corroded terminal nut at the plug
Blown fuse in the glow plug power circuit

P26A0.d: P26A0 says the exhaust glow plug system does not perform as intended, even if no electrical fault is present. Ford gives the clearest picture for the 3.2 L Transit diesel: from the 2017 summary on, the code is set when the feedback of the vaporizer glow plug relay disagrees with its command for roughly 60 s while the key is on, a fault filed under P2689 in earlier years.
s: MIL on
Exhaust temperature control code P24A0 stored too
Regenerations take longer or fail
c: Blown fuse or relay feedback not matching the command

P26A1.d: P26A1 describes a load circuit of the exhaust glow plug that reads too low: the feed or the element has found a path to ground, so the current bypasses the heater or exceeds what the circuit allows. Shorted elements, insulation damage at the hot plug body and wiring melted against the exhaust are the expected causes; a fuse in the glow plug feed may blow repeatedly.
s: MIL on
Fuse for the glow plug circuit blows again after replacement
Regeneration blocked
c: Glow element shorted to its housing
Feed wire melted or chafed against the exhaust
Fuse blown as a result of the short

P26A2.d: The high case of the exhaust glow plug load circuit is set when the monitored point sits too close to supply voltage. Depending on how the module measures, this means the heater circuit is shorted to another positive feed or the element draws almost no current, so the voltage barely drops across it.
s: MIL on
Exhaust dosing and regeneration limited
c: Glow plug feed shorted to another battery-fed circuit
Element with greatly increased resistance near the end of its life
Glow plug relay contacts stuck closed

P26A3.d: P26A3 is a functional fault: the electrics of bypass valve A look fine, but the valve does not reach or report the position it should. GM's 2011 Volt table sets it, Type B, when the end-position learn fails with coolant above 50 °C, or when the valve has not arrived at its commanded position within 15 s.
s: Check engine light on
Weak or delayed cabin heat
Unusual coolant or transmission temperatures
c: Broken gear or jammed rotor inside the bypass valve
Contaminated coolant, e.g. stop-leak additives, blocking the valve
Engine or climate control software commanding the valve incorrectly
End-position learn not completed after replacement

P26A4.d: Many electric coolant valves carry a potentiometer or Hall element that reports the actual valve angle back to the controller. P26A4 is the general circuit code for that feedback on valve A: the signal is missing or cannot be assigned to a more specific low, high or erratic fault.
s: Check engine light
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
Possible additional valve or coolant temperature codes
c: Moisture or corrosion inside the valve's position sensor section
Loose, corroded or damaged connector or feedback wiring
Missing 5 V reference or ground for the position sensor

P26A5.d: Here the feedback signal is electrically present but sits where a healthy valve should never be. In GM's 2016 Volt table the VICM treats readings between 5 and 30 % or between 70 and 95 % of the reference as invalid; 80 failures in 100 samples at 100 ms give a Type B fault, provided the drive codes P2682/P2683/P26AD/P26AE and P26A6/P26A7 are clear.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Engine runs too cool or warms up slowly
Fluctuating heater output
c: Worn or corroded position sensor track inside the valve
Damaged gear or coupling between valve motor and sensor
High contact resistance at the valve connector

P26A6.d: P26A6 means the valve A feedback voltage has dropped below its plausible floor, typically from a short to ground, a lost reference voltage or a failed sensor. GM sets it on the Volt (2011 HPC2/VICM and 2016 VICM) once the signal falls under 5 % of reference, about 0.25 V, in 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms; it is Type B, so the lamp comes on after two trips.
s: Check engine light
Delayed warm-up or reduced heater output
Valve position shown at or near zero on the scan tool
c: Feedback wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Open 5 V reference supply to the sensor
Internal sensor failure, e.g. after coolant intrusion

P26A7.d: The counterpart to P26A6: the feedback from valve A reads too high. GM's 2016 Volt table counts both a signal above its window and a broken signal circuit here, because an interrupted wire lets the input float toward the reference.
s: Check engine light
Scan tool shows valve position at maximum
Engine slow to reach operating temperature
c: Open feedback or sensor ground wire
Feedback wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Defective sensor in the valve housing

P26A8.d: P26A8 targets a feedback signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer publishes a definition for this exact code.
s: Check engine light that may come and go
Erratic heater output or engine temperature
Code returns after clearing, often on rough roads
c: Loose or spread terminal in the valve connector
Worn or contaminated sensor track giving dropouts
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting intermittently

P26A9.d: The title refers to the learned end stop of valve A. GM's use of P26A9 shifted over time.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Engine overheats or stays too cool depending on stuck position
Weak or uneven cabin heat
c: Valve rotor sticking from deposits or contaminated coolant
End position not relearned after valve or module replacement
Open motor drive circuit preventing the learn routine
Drifting position sensor misreporting the stop

P26AA.d: P26AA is the upper-limit partner of P26A9: the controller cannot confirm or learn the maximum end stop of valve A, or the reported value at full travel lies outside the expected window. No manufacturer publishes criteria for this code.
s: Check engine light
Reduced cooling under high load
Heater or engine temperature not as expected
c: Valve binding before reaching its maximum position
Worn or broken mechanical end stop or gear
Position sensor out of calibration near its upper end

P26AB.d: P26AB is stored when valve A stays open although it was told to close. Ford's hybrid summaries (2014–2019) define the valve as the switch between a combined loop, with engine coolant through the heater core, and an isolated loop heated by a PTC heater; if the second coolant sensor reads more than 5 °F above the engine sensor within 60 s of a circuit fault, the valve is judged stuck in the combined loop, and P2682 mus
s: Check engine light
Engine takes long to warm up, higher fuel use when cold
Heater works with engine off only poorly (hybrids)
c: Valve jammed open by deposits, wear or a broken drive part
Engine control software misjudging valve state (Ram flashes)
Drive circuit fault leaving the valve in its open default

P26AC.d: Which valve carries the letter B depends on the maker. Ford names it in its gasoline OBD summaries for 2020–2023 and 2024–2025: valve B is the active transmission cooling valve, which sends engine coolant to the automatic transmission oil cooler, while valve A heats the transmission.
s: Check engine light
Transmission fluid temperature higher than normal when towing
Usually no change in normal driving
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Open solenoid or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output driver in the PCM

P26AD.d: P26AD indicates a drive line of valve B pulled to ground. GM uses the code differently from the title: on the second-generation Volt (2016 table, VICM) the single coolant bypass valve has an H-bridge motor with two drive lines, and P26AD stands for driver 2 reporting a short to low while the valve is commanded toward the high position.
s: Check engine light after two drives (GM)
Valve no longer moves, heating or warm-up affected
c: Drive wire chafed and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector creating a leak path

P26AE.d: With P26AE the valve B drive output sees voltage where it expects none, typically a short to battery. GM's 2016 Volt table again applies it to the second drive line of the one bypass valve: the VICM sets it when driver 2 flags a short to high while the valve is stopped or commanded low, after 16 failures in 20 samples at 100 ms, Type B.
s: Check engine light
Valve stays in its last position
Transmission or cabin temperature control off target
c: Drive wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Internally shorted valve motor or solenoid drawing excess current
Damaged output stage in the control module

P26AF.d: P26AF is the functional fault for valve B remaining open against its command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford, for instance, monitors its valve B (transmission cooling) only electrically through P26AC/P26AE.
s: Check engine light
Longer warm-up, higher fuel use on short trips
Lower cabin heat in cold weather
c: Valve held open by deposits or debris
Seized actuator or broken drive gear
Coolant temperature sensor bias misleading the check

P26B0.d: P26B0 covers a valve B that is electrically sound but does not perform: it moves too slowly, stops short of its target or reports a position that does not match the command. No manufacturer publishes criteria for P26B0.
s: Check engine light
Engine or transmission temperature outside its normal band
c: Valve moving slowly due to contaminated or wrong coolant
Worn gear train or weak valve motor
Low supply voltage or high resistance in the drive circuit

P26B1.d: P26B1 reports that valve A does not open when it should. The best documented user is the Volkswagen group plug-in hybrids.
s: Check engine light, sometimes only intermittent
Cabin heat relies on the electric heater longer than usual
Possible rise in engine temperature under load
c: Thermal management software misjudging the valve (Porsche, Bentley)
Valve seized closed by deposits or a failed actuator
Swapped or kinked coolant lines after repair
Drifting coolant temperature sensor used for the check

P26B2.d: P26B2 is the closed-stuck counterpart for valve B: the controller expects coolant to flow through the valve but sees no sign of it. No manufacturer documents P26B2 in public sources.
s: Check engine light
Rising temperature of the component served by the valve
Possible temperature warning under heavy load
c: Valve seized in the closed position
Failed actuator motor or broken coupling
Blocked or kinked coolant line downstream of the valve

P26B3.d: Fuel shut-off valves are electrically opened valves that isolate a gaseous or liquefied fuel, as on CNG or propane systems. P26B3 says valve A does not achieve its intended effect although it was commanded.
s: Hard starting after the vehicle has been parked
Check engine light on some vehicles
Possible fuel odour
c: Leaking check valve or supply solenoid in the rail pressure module
Clogged bleed restrictor or kinked EVAP line
Shut-off valve A not switching as commanded
Blown fuse in the valve supply

P26B4.d: P26B4 is the opposite failure to P26B3: shut-off valve A stays open or energised when the module wants it closed. No manufacturer documents P26B4 in public sources.
s: Check engine light
Fuel odour after shut-off
Fuel pressure remains in the lines with the engine off
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Supply relay or driver stuck on

P26B5.d: With P26B5 shut-off valve B fails to open or pass fuel when commanded. Roush CleanTech documents the code for its Gen 4 propane system on 2016–2018 Ford trucks, where valve B is the supply solenoid in the module that regulates rail pressure (its circuit code there is P2665).
s: Engine cranks but does not start, or runs poorly
Long start sequence with pumps cycling repeatedly
Check engine light on some models
c: Supply or tank solenoid not opening
Manual valve partly closed or excess flow valve tripped
Weak fuel pumps, clogged filter or kinked lines
Blown fuse in the valve circuit

P26B6.d: P26B6 reports that shut-off valve B cannot be switched off: the control circuit or the valve remains in the on state after the module removes the command. No manufacturer documents P26B6 publicly.
s: Check engine light
Fuel odour near the engine or regulator after shut-off
c: Control line shorted to battery voltage
Welded relay contact keeping the valve powered

P26B7.d: P26B7 is the basic electrical test of the drive output for coolant bypass valve C, with an open load as its main case. The letter is not tied to one design.
s: Check engine light
Engine warms up slowly or runs warmer than usual
Valve C stays in its default position
c: Failed actuator motor or coil inside bypass valve C
Unplugged, corroded or broken connector or drive wire
Engine harness chafed through near the valve

P26B8.d: With P26B8 a drive line of valve C is pulled toward ground. The best public description comes from GM's 2025 ECM table 25OBDG04B for the six-cylinder diesel: valve C sits on an H-bridge, and the controller looks for a grounded line separately in the opening and the closing direction, each time only while the other direction is free of the same fault.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Unstable or high coolant temperature
Further valve or harness codes stored at the same time
c: Drive wire chafed against the engine or body and shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve C motor
Water or coolant in the valve connector

P26B9.d: P26B9 reports supply voltage where the valve C driver should see none, in practice a short to battery positive. Two makers document it.
s: Check engine light
Temperature gauge higher or more erratic than usual
Valve does not respond to scan tool commands
c: Drive wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Engine harness damaged by chafing or heat
Internal fault in the valve C actuator

P26BA.d: P26BA is meant for a valve C that stays open although the controller wants it shut, while its circuit tests fine. No manufacturer documents this code in public sources.
s: Check engine light
Slow warm-up and lower temperature gauge reading
Weak cabin heating in cold weather
c: Valve C jammed in the open position by wear or deposits
Dirty or mixed coolant hindering valve movement
Incorrectly learned end positions after a repair

P26BB.d: P26BB is GM's main functional code for its rotary coolant flow control valve. The ECM compares commanded and measured angle; a gap above 12° after the target has settled, or movement slower than calibrated, counts as a fault.
s: Check engine light
Coolant temperature higher or lower than normal
Code may disappear after further driving on a new valve
c: New valve still in its break-in phase (GM, low mileage)
ECM calibration needing an update per GM bulletin
Valve or actuator sticking or worn

P26BC.d: P26BC covers a valve C that will not open on command even though its drive circuit is intact. Public criteria for this code are not available from any manufacturer.
s: Check engine light
Rising engine temperature, possible overheat warning
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
c: Valve C seized in the closed position
Actuator too weak to overcome friction or deposits
Low coolant level or trapped air distorting the temperature check

P26BD.d: P26BD is the open-load or general circuit fault on the output that drives coolant bypass valve D. Ford is the documented user.
s: Check engine light
Weak or no cabin heat
Heater output that cannot be regulated
c: Open coil or motor winding in valve D
Broken drive wire between PCM and valve

P26BE.d: P26BE flags a drive circuit of valve D that reads too low, normally because the wiring or the valve itself is grounded. No manufacturer documents P26BE publicly.
s: Check engine light
Cabin heat stuck at full or at minimum
Valve D does not react to commands
c: Moisture or corrosion in the connector

P26BF.d: P26BF stands for battery voltage on the valve D control line where the driver expects a switched or grounded level. Ford documents it in its 2024–2025 gasoline OBD summary: the cabin heating bypass valve is valve D, and a short to battery reported by the PCM's smart driver is stored as P26BF, internally also as P26BD_12, after continuous monitoring for 5 s.
s: Check engine light
Heater stays hot or stays cold regardless of setting
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Harness damaged near hot or moving engine parts

P26C0.d: GM uses P26C0 for the block rotary valve, which controls coolant flow through the engine block between two mechanical end stops; its tables label it as the engine block coolant valve stuck open. The ECM counts a failure when requested and measured position differ by at least 10° while the raw feedback sits at 50° or more, i.e.
s: Check engine light
Longer warm-up, especially in cold weather
Higher fuel consumption on short trips
c: Block valve jammed on the open side
Chafed engine harness disturbing drive or feedback (GM 21-NA-149)
Position feedback reporting a wrong angle

P26C1.d: P26C1 means valve D works electrically but does not deliver the expected effect. Ford is the documented user, and on its plug-in hybrids valve D governs the cabin heating loop.
s: Check engine light
Engine overheat message in the cluster
P2183 stored at the same time
c: PCM software miscalculating heater soak time (Ford PHEV)
Contaminated connector of coolant temperature sensor 2
Valve D moving slowly or sticking

P26C2.d: P26C2 is the closed-side partner of P26C0, and GM again applies it to the block rotary valve of its engines. The test is the same comparison of commanded and actual angle, at least 10° apart in the 2019 L3B table (Type A, one trip) and 5° in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B (Type B), but here the raw feedback stays below 50°, so the valve is judged closed.
s: Check engine light, immediately on GM 2019 L3B
Rising coolant temperature or overheat warning
Reduced engine power
c: Block valve seized on the closed side
Weak actuator motor unable to open the valve

P26C3.d: P26C3 comes from a second, independent checking layer inside the powertrain module: it recalculates the gear selector position (P-R-N-D) and logs a fault when it cannot confirm what the main signal path reports. Ford lists the code in its gasoline OBD summaries 2020–2024 as non-MIL; the 2024 edition splits it into sub-faults for range sensor A, range sensor B and the comparison of both.
s: Transmission or gear selector warning in the instrument cluster
Difficulty engaging a gear or leaving Park
Further codes such as P2800 or network faults stored at the same time
c: Water ingress or corrosion in connectors of the range sensor or module wiring
Worn or misadjusted range sensor or selector giving inconsistent positions
Control module software fault, cured by a calibration update

P26C4.d: On cars with a manual gearbox, the powertrain module reads the clutch pedal through its own sensors, and an independent monitoring path inside the module checks whether that reading is credible. P26C4 is set when this check rejects the pedal information.
s: Cruise control or stop/start not available
Engine cranks only reluctantly or not at all with the pedal pressed
Service warning without check engine lamp
c: Worn or misaligned clutch pedal sensor so that sensors A and B disagree
Loose or corroded pedal sensor connector or chafed wiring
Powertrain module software needing an update

P26C5.d: Exhaust flow control valve A is the electrically driven flap that switches the sound path or back pressure of the exhaust, mostly on sporty models with selectable exhaust modes. P26C5 means the output stage driving valve A finds the circuit open or otherwise unusable.
s: Exhaust mode selection not available message
Exhaust sound no longer changes between modes
Check engine lamp on some vehicles
c: Pinched, broken or unplugged actuator wiring near the exhaust
Misaligned actuator bracket or poorly seated exhaust straining the harness
Open winding or internal fault in the valve actuator

P26C6.d: P26C6 reports that the drive circuit of exhaust valve A sits at too low a voltage – typically because the wiring or the actuator has shorted to ground. Ford's 2024 OBD summary shows that the PCM handles it as failure type 11 of the valve A circuit check, which runs continuously and needs about five seconds; the gasoline summaries 2020–2024 carry a typo here and print P25C6 instead of P26C6 in the threshold table.
s: Check engine lamp on
Exhaust mode cannot be changed
Flap stuck in one position, exhaust permanently quiet or loud
c: Control wire chafed through against the body or exhaust and shorted to ground
Internal short in the flap actuator
Water or road salt in the actuator connector

P26C7.d: P26C7 is the high-side counterpart: the control line of exhaust valve A carries more voltage than the driver expects, usually because the line touches battery positive or the actuator is damaged. In Ford's 2024 OBD summary it appears as failure type 12 of the valve A check, monitored all the time with a five-second window; the earlier summaries misprint it as P25C7 in their threshold list.
s: Check engine lamp on
Exhaust mode warning in the instrument cluster
No change in exhaust sound between modes
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered circuit
Missing ground at the actuator pulling the line high

P26C8.d: P26C8 is not a fault of the engine module itself. It is stored when a unit outside the powertrain, which the manufacturer designates chassis control module 1, has logged an emission-related code of its own and asks the engine module over the network to light the check engine lamp.
s: Check engine lamp on
Service transmission or chassis warning message
Additional codes stored in the chassis module
c: Emission-related fault stored in chassis control module 1
Replaced module with mismatched or missing software configuration
Low supply voltage or network disturbance during start-up

P26C9.d: P26C9 is the message slot for a second chassis control module: if module 2 detects an emission-related fault, it can ask the engine module to switch on the check engine lamp, and the engine module records this request as P26C9. No manufacturer documents this code in public.
s: Check engine lamp on
Codes stored in a chassis module in addition to the engine module
c: Emission-related fault stored in chassis control module 2
Incorrect configuration or software after module replacement
Low voltage or network fault corrupting the request message

P26CA.d: Many engines replace the belt-driven water pump with an electric pump that has its own control electronics. P26CA flags a fault in the control connection to that pump.
s: Check engine lamp on
Rising coolant temperature or temperature warning
Coolant traces at the electric pump
c: Water or corrosion in the pump connector or harness connectors
Coolant leaking from the pump body into its electronics
Broken control or backup run wire between module and pump

P26CB.d: P26CB means the engine coolant pump does not deliver the expected work, typically because the impeller is blocked or turns too slowly. Ford's OBD summaries for hybrids let the pump's own electronics judge this from current and speed: too much current at too low a speed through four restart attempts is reported over LIN, and the PCM records P26CB after five seconds.
s: Check engine lamp on
Cooling fans running constantly at high speed
Rising engine temperature or reduced power
c: Seized or obstructed impeller in the electric pump
Diverter shroud of a switchable mechanical pump not moving
Worn pump motor or bearing drawing excessive current
Engine module logic needing a software update

P26CC.d: P26CC reports that the circuit controlling the engine coolant pump stays at too low a voltage while the pump should be active. Honda uses the code on its two-motor hybrids and calls it a low voltage in the circuit of the electric pump: service bulletin 25-020 (Accord and CR-V Hybrid 2023–2024, Civic Hybrid 2025) explains that moisture in the pump relay can freeze at or below 0 °C, the relay then fails to switch, the
s: Check engine lamp on after a cold start
Poor cabin heating or rising engine temperature
c: Moisture inside the pump relay freezing in cold weather
Pump control or supply wire shorted to ground
Blown fuse or poor supply to the relay

P26CD.d: P26CD is set when the control circuit of the engine coolant pump shows a higher voltage than the commanded state allows, for example while the driver is switched off. No manufacturer documents this code in public.
s: Check engine lamp on
Pump running after the engine is switched off
Longer warm-up phase
c: Pump control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open ground at the pump pulling the circuit high

P26CE.d: P26CE covers a pump that spins too fast for the current it draws – a sign that it is running dry or pumping air instead of coolant. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries spell out the check: the electronics in the pump report a dry-run state over LIN when speed exceeds 4,909 rpm while current stays too low, and the PCM sets the code after five seconds.
s: Coolant temperature warning in the cluster
Check engine lamp on
Gurgling noises or poor heater output
c: Low coolant level from a leak
Air pockets left after coolant service or pump replacement
Impeller loose or broken on the pump shaft

P26CF.d: Smart coolant pumps carry their own electronics, which measure the supply voltage they receive. P26CF is the general code for that voltage when it is implausible but cannot be assigned to too low or too high.
s: Check engine lamp on
Other voltage-related codes stored at the same time
c: Loose, corroded or intermittent pump supply or ground connection
Weak battery or charging system fault
Faulty voltage measurement in the pump electronics

P26D0.d: P26D0 means the electronics in the engine coolant pump see less voltage than they should. On Ford's 2.0 L hybrids (C-Max, Fusion, MKZ) the pump module reports its electronics voltage over LIN, the PCM compares it with the battery voltage it measures itself and sets the code when the gap reaches about four volts for five seconds.
s: Check engine lamp on
Network codes such as U019F stored alongside
Rising engine temperature under load
c: Water or corrosion in a connector of the pump supply
High resistance in the pump ground or feed wire
Weak 12 V battery or low charging voltage

P26D1.d: P26D1 is stored when the electronics of the engine coolant pump report a supply voltage clearly above the vehicle system voltage. Ford documents the check in its OBD summaries for hybrid and plug-in models: the pump module passes its measured electronics voltage on via the LIN link, and a reading more than about four volts above the battery voltage seen by the PCM for five seconds sets P26D1.
s: Check engine lamp on
Unusually bright lights or other overvoltage codes
c: Faulty voltage regulator or overvoltage from jump starting
Poor PCM ground making the reference voltage look low
Voltage measurement drift inside the pump electronics

P26D2.d: The electronics of a smart coolant pump also measure their own temperature. P26D2 is set when this value climbs too high: in Ford's hybrid OBD summaries the pump module reports the temperature over LIN and the PCM stores P26D2 once it passes 130 °C for five seconds.
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine temperature rising or temperature warning
Reduced heater output
c: Low coolant level or air around the pump reducing cooling of its electronics
Stiff impeller or bearing making the motor draw high current
Internal fault in the pump electronics or temperature sensor

P26D3.d: P26D3 concerns the power feed and ground of the engine coolant pump. On Ford's 2.0 L hybrids the pump module has no way of reporting a loss of these lines, since without power it goes quiet on the LIN bus.
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine temperature climbing quickly
U019F stored at the same time
c: Blown pump fuse or failed supply relay
Broken power feed or loose ground at the pump
Pump electronics dead so that the pump neither runs nor communicates

P26D4.d: P26D4 narrows the supply fault of the engine coolant pump down to too low a voltage on its power feed. There is no public manufacturer documentation for this code.
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluctuating engine temperature or heater output
c: Corroded fuse holder or connector in the pump feed
Partial short to ground on the feed wire

P26D5.d: P26D5 is set when the power feed of the engine coolant pump carries a higher voltage than the system allows. No manufacturer documents this code in public.
s: Check engine lamp on
Overvoltage codes in other control modules
c: Supply relay stuck closed so the feed stays live
Feed or sensing wire shorted to another powered circuit

P26D6.d: Some engines drive their mechanical coolant pump through a switchable clutch: following a cold start the pump is left idle so the coolant stays still and the engine reaches temperature sooner, and once a target is met the clutch couples the pump to its drive again. P26D6 means the engine control module sees the control circuit of this clutch as open – typically a broken wire, a loose connector or a solenoid coil that
s: Check engine light on
Engine and cabin heater take longer to warm up
Coolant temperature behaves differently from normal after a cold start
c: Broken wire or corroded, loose connector in the clutch control circuit
Open solenoid coil in the coolant pump clutch
Blown fuse or missing supply to the clutch solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P26D7.d: P26D7 is the serious case for a clutched coolant pump: the module has asked the clutch to couple the pump, but the cooling system shows no sign of circulation, so the pump is assumed to stay disconnected. The electrical side may be intact; worn friction faces, a seized armature or a pump that slips under load are typical mechanical reasons.
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature rises quickly, possible overheating warning
Radiator fans run at high speed
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
c: Worn or slipping clutch friction surfaces
Armature or switching mechanism seized in the disengaged position
Slipping or damaged pump drive belt
Implausible coolant temperature input or outdated engine software

P26D8.d: With P26D8 the opposite of the warm-up strategy happens: the engine module wants the coolant pump decoupled after a cold start, but the pump keeps turning, so coolant circulates from the first second and the engine warms up as slowly as with a plain belt-driven pump. Behind this are usually a clutch that has welded or jammed shut, a return spring that no longer works or a control line that stays energised in designs
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up, heater gets warm late
Slightly higher fuel consumption on short trips
c: Clutch mechanically jammed or welded in the engaged position
Weak return spring or demagnetised holding magnet
No current at the solenoid in designs that need current to disengage

P26D9.d: P26D9 narrows the electrical fault of the coolant pump clutch down to a control line that sits too close to ground. The output stage in the engine module notices that the voltage on the line stays low when it should be high, which almost always points to a chafed wire touching the engine block or body, a coil with shorted turns, or water in a connector near the pump.
s: Check engine light on
Changed warm-up behaviour of the engine
Possibly a blown fuse with further faults on the same circuit
c: Chafed control wire shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant in the connector at the pump

P26DA.d: P26DA is the high-side counterpart of P26D9: the control line of the coolant pump clutch shows more voltage than the commanded state permits, for instance while the driver should be pulling it low or while it is switched off. Typical causes are a wire rubbing against a live circuit, a missing ground at the clutch so the line floats up, or an open coil that the driver reads as high.
s: Check engine light on
Pump clutch does not switch, warm-up or cooling behaves differently
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Open ground or poor ground contact at the clutch solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P26DB.d: Some sporty cars shape the sound reaching the cabin or the tailpipe with an electrically driven part, such as a switchable flap in the silencer or a valve in an intake sound pipe. Circuit A is the first of up to two such actuators.
s: Check engine light, depending on the manufacturer
Sport sound or valve opening no longer noticeable
Driving behaviour otherwise unchanged
c: Actuator connector unplugged or not fully seated, often after exhaust or intake work
Broken wire near the hot exhaust or at a moving section of the harness
Internal open circuit in the sound valve or actuator
Sound component removed or replaced by an aftermarket part without electrical equivalent

P26DC.d: P26DC reports that the control line of sound actuator A sits at too low a voltage, which points to the wire or the actuator being grounded rather than interrupted. Depending on the design, the driver stage then cannot switch the flap or valve, or switches it permanently because the ground path bypasses it.
s: Check engine light
Exhaust or intake sound does not change between driving modes
Possibly a blown fuse for the actuator circuit
c: Control wire chafed through and touching body or exhaust metal
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Shorted winding inside the sound actuator
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P26DD.d: With P26DD the module measures a voltage on the drive line of sound actuator A that is higher than the switching state allows. The usual reason is contact with a live conductor, for instance a neighbouring supply wire in a melted harness, or an internal fault in the actuator that feeds battery voltage back.
s: Check engine light
Valve stays in one position, sound permanently loud or quiet
c: Drive wire shorted to a supply wire, often where heat has damaged the harness
Internal fault in the actuator feeding voltage back into the drive line
Incorrect or aftermarket actuator with different electrical layout
Output stage of the controlling module defective

P26DE.d: Unlike the pure wiring codes, P26DE means the circuit of sound actuator A is electrically intact but the part does not behave as commanded, for example a flap that sticks, moves too slowly or reports an implausible position. The best documented case is Nissan's GT-R: bulletin NTB19-036, last amended in 2023 for model years 2017 to 2020, sets the check engine lamp with P26DE and names the electric control valve on the
s: Check engine light
Exhaust note no longer changes, or changes late
Rattling or buzzing from the silencer area
c: Exhaust sound valve sticking or worn
Engine software with too strict an evaluation, update available from the maker
Flap linkage blocked by deposits, ice or damage
Weak actuator motor or faulty position feedback

P26DF.d: Sensor power supplies A to D are separate outputs of a control module that feed groups of sensors; they are a different family from the 5 V sensor reference voltages (P0641 and following). D is the fourth such output.
s: Check engine light
Several sensor codes stored together
Reduced power or emergency mode depending on the sensors affected
c: Broken supply wire or splice to the sensors on output D
Loose or corroded pin at the control module or a sensor
Supply output D inside the control module failed

P26E0.d: P26E0 means the fourth sensor supply output of the control module is pulled below its normal level. Deutz documents it for the fourth ECU sensor supply, SPN 3512, in two variants: excessive current or a grounded circuit (FMI 6), and a reading below the physical limit with top severity (FMI 1).
s: Check engine light
Group of sensor faults appearing at once
Engine derate or emergency mode
c: One sensor on supply D with an internal short pulling the output down
Supply wire chafed and touching engine ground
Moisture in a sensor plug bridging supply and ground

P26E1.d: With P26E1 the fourth sensor supply of the control module reads higher than its regulated value. Deutz assigns it to SPN 3512 with FMI 0, meaning a reading beyond the upper physical limit, rated as most severe.
s: Check engine light
Implausible readings from several sensors
Possible derate depending on the sensors involved
c: Supply D wire shorted to battery voltage or a higher supply
Faulty sensor feeding voltage back into the supply rail
Regulator for supply D in the control module defective

P26E2.d: Bi-fuel vehicles show the active fuel with an indicator, often a lamp in the selector switch. GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel lights it while running on CNG and flashes it during a fuel change; GM's 2016 CNG pickups also flash it fast to signal a gas system fault, and Ford's earlier bi-fuel trucks combined the ALT/GAS selector with its lamp in one assembly.
s: Fuel mode lamp dark or permanently lit
No visible warning when the gas system has a fault
c: Lamp control wire chafed to ground
Shorted LED or bulb in the fuel selector switch
Faulty lamp output in the controlling module

P26E3.d: P26E3 is the opposite case of P26E2: the module that drives the fuel mode lamp sees a voltage on its control line that is higher than its commanded state allows. With a ground-side driver this is usually a short to a 12 V feed, or an open lamp that lets the line float to supply level; with a positive-side driver it points to outside voltage reaching the output.
s: Fuel mode lamp stays dark
Driver cannot tell which fuel is in use
c: Lamp control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Burnt-out bulb or open LED in the selector switch
Damaged or wet connector at the selector switch

P26E4.d: Stop-start systems often use a second starter relay, and P26E4 is the general circuit fault of this relay B. On GM's 12 V stop-start engines it switches the pinion of a tandem starter: the module's high-side driver flags an open circuit when, at standstill with at least 11 V, more than 200 kOhm appear toward ground in 40 of 50 samples (50 ms each); type B, so the lamp lights after two trips.
s: Check engine light
Engine does not restart from an automatic stop
Stop-start function disabled, occasional no-crank
c: Open wire or loose terminal between module and relay B or pinion solenoid
Control module software misjudging the circuit, update available on some FCA models
Open coil in relay B or in the tandem starter pinion solenoid
Faulty high-side driver in the engine module

P26E5.d: P26E5 indicates that the control circuit of starter relay B is shorted against ground. GM documents it for the tandem starter pinion relay of its 12 V stop-start engines: while the driver is switched on, an impedance of 0.5 Ohm or less toward ground in 8 of 10 samples of 50 ms sets the code, enabled at standstill once run/crank voltage is at least 6.41 V; the lamp follows as type B after two trips.
s: Check engine light
No crank or no restart after an automatic engine stop
Blown fuses and further unrelated codes if a harness short is the cause
c: Engine harness chafed so the relay B control wire touches ground
Shorted coil in relay B or the pinion solenoid
Damaged high-side driver in the engine module

P26E6.d: P26E6 reports a short to positive on the control line of starter relay B. GM tests for it while its driver for the tandem starter pinion relay is off: if the line still shows 0.5 Ohm or less toward a power source for 40 out of 50 checks taken every 50 ms, with the engine stopped and at least 11 V available, the code is stored as type B.
s: Check engine light
Stop-start disabled
Starter noise or grinding without a start command
c: Relay B control wire shorted to a battery-powered wire, e.g. under the battery tray
Relay B internally fed or contacts welded
Engine module driver output not switching off

P26E7.d: Supply D is the fourth switched rail with which a control module powers a group of solenoids or other loads, after A (P0657), B (P2669) and C (P2684). P26E7 reports an open load on it.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Transmission stays in a substitute gear or limp mode
Several solenoid or clutch codes stored at the same time
c: Broken wire or loose, corroded connector between the module output and the loads on supply D
Open coil in a solenoid powered from this rail
Internal fault in the high-side output of the transmission control module

P26E8.d: P26E8 says the voltage on supply rail D drops too far while the rail is switched on. In GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables this is watched continuously at high-side output 8: a timer runs when the voltage falls below a share of the supply or the averaged current is too high, and after 60 ms the code is set, Type A; it is suspended while P0882 or P0883 is present.
s: Warning light on, often only briefly or intermittently
Transmission failsafe mode with loss of the solenoids on that rail
On trucks, lost communication with NOx, PM and DEF sensors and a derate warning
c: Supply line or a connected load shorted to ground
Loose or corroded battery, fuse or ground connections feeding the module, or weak batteries (Volvo/Mack aftertreatment module)
Faulty sensor or solenoid on the rail drawing too much current
Internal fault in the module output stage

P26E9.d: The high fault of rail D is about voltage where none should be: the controller has turned supply D off, yet the line stays live. Either the high-side switch inside the module no longer opens or an outside wire touches battery positive.
s: Warning light on after two drive cycles
Transmission in limp mode or with restricted gears
Code appears after restarting rather than while driving
c: High-side switch in the control module stuck closed
Supply D wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water or corrosion in the module connector creating a leakage path

P26EA.d: Vehicles with a second fuel pump give it its own driver module, and P26EA means that module B has reported an internal fault of its own. Ford documents the code in its gasoline OBD summary for 2020 to 2023 and again in 2024 as an internal error reported by the driver module of pump B.
s: Warning light on, depending on the vehicle calibration
Hesitation or power loss at high load
Hard starting or stalling if the second pump is needed
c: Internal failure of fuel pump driver module B
Open or corroded fuel pump monitor wire between module B and the PCM or relay module
Poor power or ground at module B
Worn or seized fuel pump B overloading the module

P26EB.d: On bi-fuel engines a separate alternative fuel control module often runs the gas side. In Ford's bi-fuel CNG documentation of 2002 it contains drivers for both injector sets, switches the fuel relays, picks the active fuel from the selector switch and shuts the tank valve when gas pressure falls below 517 kPa.
s: Gas mode not available or vehicle switches back to gasoline
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a fault
Warning light on
c: Loose, corroded or undersized power or ground connection at the gas control module
Faulty fuse, relay or feed circuit of the gas system
Weak battery or alternator voltage outside the normal range
Internal fault in the alternative fuel control module

P26EC.d: Where a vehicle has two sound actuators, for instance one flap per tailpipe side or a valve in addition to an intake sound tube, B designates the second one. P26EC is stored when its drive circuit is broken, so switching the output produces no current.
s: Check engine light, depending on the manufacturer
Sound changes only on one side or not at all
c: Connector of the second actuator loose or disconnected
Wire to actuator B broken, for example by heat or vibration

P26ED.d: P26ED concerns the second sound actuator and indicates a drive line pulled toward ground. A conductor rubbed bare on the exhaust bracket, a pinched loom or corrosion bridging the pins of a wet plug are the classic culprits, along with a shorted coil inside the actuator.
s: Check engine light
Second flap does not respond, sound only partly changes
c: Insulation of the actuator B wire worn through against metal
Corroded or wet connector at actuator B

P26EE.d: For the second sound actuator, P26EE signals a drive circuit carrying more voltage than expected, i.e. a short to battery positive or a feed coming back from a damaged actuator.
s: Check engine light
Second flap stuck in one position
c: Actuator B wire in contact with a positive supply wire
Damaged actuator B feeding voltage back
Faulty output stage for circuit B in the module

P26EF.d: P26EF is the functional fault of the second sound actuator: wiring checks pass, yet flap or valve B does not reach or report the commanded state in time. No maker documents P26EF publicly.
s: Check engine light
Sound of the second branch changes late or not at all
Rattle from the flap housing
c: Flap B binding due to soot, rust or a seized shaft
Worn gearbox or weak motor in actuator B
Evaluation in the module software too sensitive

P26F0.d: P26F0 says that starter relay A remains closed even though the module has withdrawn its command, so current keeps flowing to the starter or its solenoid. Unlike the circuit codes P0615 to P0617, the wiring may be intact; the problem lies in the switching itself, typically welded contacts or a sticking armature.
s: Starter keeps running or grinding after the engine has started
Check engine light, stop-start disabled
Burning smell or flat battery after short trips
c: Welded or sticking contacts in starter relay A
Relay A control circuit fed from elsewhere so the coil stays energised
Faulty crank feedback signal suggesting a closed relay

P26F1.d: P26F1 is the opposite case to P26F0: the module commands starter relay A on, but the expected reaction never arrives, so the starter receives no power. Possible reasons are burnt or contaminated contacts, a coil that no longer pulls in, or a missing feed on the load side, for example a blown fuse or a loose battery cable at the relay.
s: Engine does not crank, or only after several attempts
Check engine light
No restart after an automatic stop
c: Burnt or dirty contacts in starter relay A
Blown fuse or loose power cable on the load side of the relay
Relay coil no longer pulling in
Feedback wire to the module interrupted

P26F2.d: P26F2 concerns the second starter relay, which on stop-start vehicles may engage the pinion of a tandem starter (GM) or form the second switching path of a two-relay layout (FCA Starter Control 2). The code means relay B fails to drop out after its command ends.
s: Grinding or whining from the starter after the engine runs
Check engine light, stop-start unavailable
c: Contacts of relay B welded or stuck
Control line of relay B fed from another circuit
Pinion solenoid of the tandem starter sticking mechanically

P26F3.d: P26F3 reports that starter relay B does not switch through when commanded, so the start sequence that depends on it cannot complete. It is the one code of this group with a public manufacturer case: an FCA STAR case for the Jeep Gladiator, released in March 2022, describes a check engine light and a no-start with P26F3, P00FD and P0562 stored, caused by loose power cables at the power control relay; tightening them t
s: Check engine light
Engine does not start or crank
Further codes for low system voltage or battery state
c: Loose power cable at the relay or power distribution unit
Burnt contacts in starter relay B
Weak battery or low system voltage so the relay does not pull in

P26F4.d: Coolant pump C is a third electric pump next to pumps A and B; which circuit it serves is defined by each manufacturer. In Bentley's V8 models from the Volkswagen group it is the auxiliary pump for the heater circuit, while GM's diesel tables use the C codes for the pump of the low-temperature loop.
s: Check engine light on
Weak cabin heating at idle or with the engine stopped
Higher charge air or component temperatures, depending on the loop
c: Broken control wire or loose connector at pump C
Corroded pins from road splash or coolant ingress
Internal electronics of the pump failed

P26F5.d: P26F5 reports that the control circuit of coolant pump C is pulled too low. Bentley documents the code in the engine electronics of the Continental GT/GTC and Flying Spur.
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable change in heating or engine behaviour
Fault may come and go (stored as intermittent)
c: Internal corrosion of the pump causing a short circuit
Over-sensitive internal diagnosis of the pump (known pump part number)
Control wire shorted to ground or coolant in the connector

P26F6.d: P26F6 is stored when the control line of coolant pump C carries a higher voltage than the commanded state allows. In practice that means the wire touches a live circuit, the pump has lost its ground so the line floats up, or the line is open between driver and pump in a way the output stage reads as high.
s: Check engine light on
Pump runs on after switch-off or does not run at all
Weak heater output with the engine idling
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Missing or corroded ground at pump C
Internal electronics of the pump failed

P26F7.d: Unlike P26F4 to P26F6, which concern the control signal, P26F7 points to the power feed of coolant pump C: the voltage arriving at the pump is missing or implausible. A blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a broken feed wire or a loose ground are the usual causes; a weak battery during cranking can also trigger it.
s: Check engine light on
Pump C does not run at all
Further codes for the same fuse or for low voltage
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump C feed
Broken feed wire or loose, corroded ground
Low system voltage from a weak battery or charging fault

P26F8.d: P26F8 is about mechanics rather than wiring: coolant pump C is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn or stops under load. Smart pumps recognise this themselves from a high motor current at little or no speed, and report it to the controlling module.
s: Check engine light on
Heating or component cooling of the affected loop fails
Pump may hum without turning
c: Seized bearing or rotor in pump C
Debris or deposits in the pump from contaminated coolant
Frozen coolant from an incorrect mixture

P26F9.d: Electric coolant pumps carry their own control electronics, which are cooled by the liquid passing through the pump. P26F9 means the electronics of pump C have reported a temperature above their limit.
s: Check engine light on
Pump C runs at reduced speed or switches off temporarily
Heating or cooling of the affected loop varies
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in pump C
Partly blocked impeller causing high current
Faulty temperature sensing in the pump electronics

P26FA.d: P26FA flags a coolant pump C that turns far faster than it should – the classic sign of a pump moving air instead of liquid. GM uses the code in the engine module of its diesel calibrations for the pump of the low-temperature coolant loop: in table 20OBDG04 an actual speed of at least 4,500 rpm in 5 of 8 one-second samples sets it, in 25OBDG04A 4 of 5 samples suffice.
s: Check engine light on after two trips
Gurgling from the pump area
Higher charge air temperature and possibly reduced power
c: Low coolant level or air left in the low-temperature loop after service
Leak in the loop drawing in air
Chafed engine harness corrupting pump signals
Impeller slipping on its shaft or broken

P26FB.d: A diesel engine routes recirculated exhaust around the EGR cooler while it is cold, so that the gas warms the engine and aftertreatment; later the bypass flap closes and the gas passes through the cooler. P26FB means the bypass on bank 1 does not open when commanded and stays in the closed, cooling position.
s: Check engine light on
Longer warm-up of engine and exhaust aftertreatment
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Blocked orifice or kinked vacuum line to the bypass actuator
Bypass flap sticking from soot and deposits
Faulty vacuum solenoid or weak vacuum supply
Outdated PCM calibration with too sensitive detection

P26FC.d: P26FC is the bank 2 version of P26FB and only exists on engines with a separate EGR cooler and bypass for each cylinder bank, typically V-configuration diesels. The engine module has commanded the bypass of the second bank open, but position feedback or the resulting gas temperature shows it is still closed, so the exhaust gas keeps flowing through the cooler during warm-up.
s: Check engine light on
Slower warm-up of the exhaust aftertreatment
c: Blocked, leaking or kinked vacuum line to the bank 2 actuator
Bypass flap of bank 2 sticking from soot deposits

P26FD.d: Electric A/C compressors in hybrids and electric vehicles carry their own inverter and control electronics. P26FD says this built-in module does not work as expected, as judged by the module that supervises the compressor.
s: Check engine light on without a code in the engine module
Air conditioning weak or not cooling
Further A/C codes stored as sporadic
c: Software error in the climate or compressor control
Internal electronics or inverter of the compressor failing
Fault in the high-voltage supply or fuse of the compressor

P26FE.d: P26FE concerns the electrically driven exhaust flap A on models with selectable exhaust sound. The circuit is fine, but the flap does not reach the commanded position.
s: Check engine light on
Message that exhaust or drive mode is not available
No audible change in exhaust sound between modes
c: Flap sticking from corrosion, soot or freezing moisture
Exhaust or actuator bracket not seated correctly
Actuator not aligned after replacement or outdated PCM software

P26FF.d: Some engine controllers set themselves up at power-on by checking which inputs are connected, so one module can serve several engine layouts. On V engines with a separate throttle body for each cylinder bank this includes a throttle position signal per bank.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced engine power or limp mode
Poor throttle response or rough idle
c: Bank 2 throttle body connector unplugged or not fully seated
Open signal, reference or ground wire to the bank 2 throttle position sensor
Engine controller programmed or replaced with software for a different engine variant
